📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You've got everything ready - data, model, a beefy GPU setup. You hit "run" and... wait. And wait some more. Your GPUs are barely breaking a sweat while your wallet's getting lighter by the hour.

According to recent reports, sound familiar? We've been there. After some detective work on our nanoVLM project, we discovered the real culprit wasn't our model or hardware, it was our data pipeline being incredibly wasteful.

In this post we build an efficient pipeline in five stages. In each stage we add or remove from the previous step and comment on what went right and what did not.

According to recent reports, to make it easier to follow the data preparation tasks, we created a separate repo laser-focused on the data pipeline only. We hope this will be much easier to understand that reading the code once integrated with the nanoVLM repository. In addition, this could be useful to bootstrap other data pipelines!

Repository: https://github.com/ariG23498/mmdp.

According to recent reports, to follow along, all you need to do is clone the repository. It contains the final data preparation tasks, but it's designed to showcase each step of the way.

Before optimizing anything, we need to understand what we are working with. Our multimodal dataset has images, text prompts, and responses.

Getting familiar with your training data is crucial for success. The previous script indicates a random sample each time you run it; you may want to copy the snippet to a notebook and run it multiple times to get a feeling about the data.

Our first training attempt used the obvious (and very frequent) approach:.

In a recent development, the results were painful. Look at this visualization:.

See all that gray? That's padding. That's the GPU processing absolutely nothing while you pay for compute time. We were wasting roughly 60% of our batch on empty tokens.

Recent findings suggest that our next move was simple. Set a global maximum length and stick to it. If a sample was too long, we'd just drop it.

According to recent reports, as you might have noticed that the batch now has one sample less. This is due to the filtering process. This helped, but we were still padding everything to the same fixed length regardless of actual content. Better than before, but still wasteful.

Now we’re ready to rethink batching entirely. Padding is the enemy, and we need a strategy to minimize it while maximizing how much data we can fit into each batch. Enter the knapsack problem, a classic from computer science that’s perfect for this.

In a recent development, imagine you’re packing a backpack for a hike. It can only hold so much weight, and you want to cram in as many useful items as possible. In our case:.

To test this idea, we start with a toy dataset: just a list of numbers from 1 to 25, each representing a sequence length. This lets us experiment without the complexity of images and text.

It has been revealed that most PyTorch datasets are map-style (you access them with dataset[i]). But for dynamic batching, we need something more flexible. So, we built an iterable-style dataset by subclassing torch.utils.data.IterableDataset. This lets us generate batches on the fly and handle tricks like sharding data across multiple workers:.

In a recent development, packing sequences can be slow, especially if we’re sorting or shuffling. To keep things moving, we use a producer-consumer pattern using Python queues:.

The producer thread packs batches and puts them in a queue, while the main thread pulls them out as needed. This overlap keeps the pipeline flowing smoothly.

First, we try a simple greedy packing strategy:.

According to recent reports, this walks through the data sequentially, adding items to a pack until it’s full, then starting a fresh one. It’s fast but not perfect. Here’s what the batches look like:.

Notice how later batches get sparse? We’re leaving gaps.

Let’s try a smarter approach: bin-packing (specifically, First Fit Decreasing):.

Recent findings suggest that this sorts sequences by length (longest first) and tries to fit each one into the first pack that has room. If none fits, it starts a upcoming pack. The result?

According to recent reports, these batches are much tighter, with less wasted space. It’s like playing Tetris with your data, fitting pieces together snugly.

Now for the real deal, applying knapsack packing to our multimodal dataset.

We’re back to images, prompts, and responses, and we need to pack them efficiently while respecting both token limits and image budgets. Image budgeting is done so that images per sample are balanced. We would like to avoid the case where one GPU needs to process way more images than another.

In a recent development, our newly introduced ConstantLengthDataset class handles the heavy lifting. Here’s how it works, compared to Stage 4:.

The ConstantLengthDataset does it all:.

Look at that! The gray (padding) is minimal, and the batches are dense with useful data. It’s like packing a suitcase so well you can still zip it up without sitting on it.

The image might seem unintuive at the first glance, but let us look at the image side by side with constrained padding.

Here you will notice that the samples in knapsack are more evenly distributed. We also do not run into the problem of having less samples in the batch due to filtering.

What started as a simple "why is training so slow?" investigation led to a complete rethink of how we handle multimodal data.

The balanced knapsack strategy for data pipeline comes from the Eagle 2: Building Post-Training Data Strategies from Scratch for Frontier Vision-Language Models paper from NVIDIA.

Happy training (and may your GPUs stay busy)!

The problem with strong passwords isn’t understanding why you need them; it’s keeping track of a different one for every account.

That’s useful whether you’re creating an account for a single purchase or signing into a service you use every day.

It has been revealed that unique passwords also help limit the fallout from a data breach. If a retailer exposes your login credentials, using a different password elsewhere means those same credentials won’t unlock your other accounts.

With unlimited logins and encrypted vaults that sync across devices, Proton Pass lets you keep those details together as you move between your phone and computer.

It has been revealed that proton Pass is available for practically every platform, from Chrome and Firefox on the web to native macOS, Windows, and Linux apps to, of course, iOS and Android. Black Friday shopping often leaves something behind long after the packages arrive: a steady stream of promotional emails from stores you barely remember visiting.

Proton Pass includes unlimited hide-my-email aliases, giving you an alternative to handing out your real address every time you create an account.

According to recent reports, an alias is an extra email address that forwards messages to your normal inbox. You can give it to a shopping website and still receive your order confirmations and delivery updates, without sharing the underlying address you use for everything else.

If that alias starts receiving spam, you can switch it off. Your real email address stays the same, and you don’t have to update all your other accounts.

Recent findings suggest that it’s a practical way to put some distance between your primary inbox and the websites you’re trying for the first time. A separate alias for each service also gives you more control: you can stop messages arriving through one address without disrupting the others.

Passwords are only part of what’s worth keeping in a secure, accessible place.

According to recent reports, proton Pass also stores notes, credit card details, and other confidential information in end-to-end encrypted vaults. That makes it useful for the small, everyday moments when you need something sensitive and don’t want to go looking for it.

When you’re booking a flight, saved passport details let you look up the information you need without digging through a drawer halfway through the reservation.

When you’re shopping online, saved card details mean you don’t have to leave the checkout page to find your wallet.

When you’re traveling, keeping a digital copy of an important document within reach gives you a convenient reference while you’re away from home. It doesn’t replace an original document where one is required, but it can save you from searching through scattered files and messages.

Pass Plus is the straightforward choice for one person who wants password generation, autofill, unlimited aliases, and secure storage.

According to recent reports, pass Family includes six Pass Plus accounts and a family admin panel. If several people in your household need a password manager, it’s worth considering rather than setting everyone up with separate subscriptions.

According to recent reports, proton Unlimited bundles Pass with Proton VPN, Proton Mail, Proton Drive, and more, including 500 GB of cloud storage. It’s the option to consider if you also want a VPN, encrypted email, and cloud storage alongside your password manager.

A password manager isn’t the most conspicuous Black Friday purchase, but it’s one you can put to work immediately: the next account you create, the next password you forget, or the next time a checkout asks for details you don’t have handy.

Modern text-to-speech systems turn written words into audio through several stages.

Sources indicate that newer expressive systems go further by reading the whole script to infer emotion and context, and by accepting direction in the text itself, such as a bracketed note that says to whisper. That is why a single script can produce very different reads depending on the model and the instructions.

If you use a tool with SSML support, you can make a spoken code or number far clearer:.

Recent findings suggest that the say-as element tells the engine to read the number digit by digit, and the break and emphasis tags shape the rhythm. Supported tags and attributes differ between engines, so check the documentation for yours.

In a recent development, what is the best AI text to speech tool? It depends on the job. OpenArt suits voiceovers with video and music, ElevenLabs suits expressive multilingual audio, Murf AI suits studio-style control, Speechify suits listening, WellSaid Labs suits licensed corporate work and Amazon Polly suits developers.

It has been revealed that is AI text to speech free? Several tools offer free intends or credits, but limits are common. Examples include OpenArt’s free credits for new accounts, ElevenLabs’ free monthly credits and Murf’s limited free initiative, which has no commercial licence.

In a recent development, can AI text to speech clone my voice? Some tools support it, including OpenArt and ElevenLabs, usually from a short recording of your own voice. Only clone voices you have permission to use.

What is SSML? Speech Synthesis Markup Language is a W3C standard that lets you control pauses, emphasis, pronunciation and pitch in synthetic speech. Amazon Polly is one service that supports it.

Which tool is best for developers? Amazon Polly and ElevenLabs both offer APIs, and Murf describes API options as well. Evaluate latency, languages, pricing and SDK support for your use case.

How do I make AI voices sound less robotic? Write conversationally, add pauses and emphasis, correct pronunciations and split long scripts into short sections. Choose a model that is designed for expressive reads.

Latest Update: Three Mighty Alerts Supporting Hugging Face’s Production Infrastructure

📅 08 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3005 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Infrastructure team at Hugging Face is excited to share a behind-the-scenes look at the inner workings of Hugging Face's production infrastructure, which we’ve had the privilege of helping to build and maintain.
  • In this blog post, we’ll dive into the details of three mighty alerts that play their unique role in supporting our production infrastructure, and explore how they've helped us maintain the high level of performance and uptime that our community relies on.
  • Oftentimes, with cloud computing architectures, where data flows between private and public networks, implementing a NAT (Network Address Translation) gateway stands as a steadfast best practice.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Infrastructure team at Hugging Face is excited to share a behind-the-scenes look at the inner workings of Hugging Face's production infrastructure, which we’ve had the privilege of helping to build and maintain. Our team's dedication to designing and implementing a robust monitoring and alerting system has been instrumental in ensuring the stability and scalability of our platforms. We’re constantly reminded of the impact that our alerts have on our ability to identify and respond to potential challenges before they become major incidents.

In this blog post, we’ll dive into the details of three mighty alerts that play their unique role in supporting our production infrastructure, and explore how they've helped us maintain the high level of performance and uptime that our community relies on.

Oftentimes, with cloud computing architectures, where data flows between private and public networks, implementing a NAT (Network Address Translation) gateway stands as a steadfast best practice. This gateway acts as a strategic gatekeeper, monitoring and facilitating all outbound traffic towards the public Internet. By centralizing egress traffic, the NAT gateway offers a strategic vantage point for comprehensive visibility. Our team can easily query and analyze this traffic, making it an invaluable asset when working through security, cost optimization or various other investigative scenarios.

According to recent reports, cost optimization is a critical aspect of cloud infrastructure management, and understanding the pricing dynamics is key. In data centers, pricing structures often differentiate between east-west traffic (typically communication within the same rack or building) and north-south traffic (communication between further away private networks or the internet). By monitoring network traffic volume, Hugging Face gains valuable insights into these traffic patterns. This awareness allows us to make informed decisions regarding infrastructure configuration and architecture, ensuring we limit incurring needless costs.

Sources indicate that one of our key alerts is designed to notify us when our network traffic volume surpasses a predefined threshold. This alert serves multiple purposes. Firstly, it acts as an early warning system, alerting us to any unusual spikes in traffic that might indicate potential problems or unexpected behavior. Secondly, it prompts us to regularly review our traffic trends, ensuring we stay on top of our infrastructure's growth and evolving needs. This alert is set at a static threshold, which we have fine-tuned over time, ensuring it remains relevant and effective. When triggered, it often coincides with periods of refactoring our infrastructure.

For instance, when integrating third-party security and autoscaling tools, we've observed increased telemetry data egress from our nodes, triggering the alert and prompting us to optimize our configurations.

On another occasion, adjustments to our infrastructure lead to mistakenly avoiding a private, low-cost path between product-specific infrastructure (ex. traffic destined to the Hub from a Space to interact with repository data). To elaborate further, the most impactful workloads in terms of cost savings we’ve found are those that access object storage. Fetching objects directly prices cheaper than going through CDN-hosted assets for our LFS repository storage and additionally does not require the same security measures that our WAF provides compared to public requests arriving at our front door. Leveraging DNS overrides to switch traffic through private network paths and public network paths has become a valuable technique for us, driven by the CDKTF AWS provider.

As a final note, while we have configuration-as-code ensuring the desired state is always in effect, having an additional layer of alerting around helps in case mistakes are made when expressing the desired state through code.

Industry observers note that the logging infrastructure at Hugging Face is a sophisticated system designed to collect, process, and store vast amounts of log data generated by our applications and services. At the heart of this system is the Hub application logging pipeline, a well-architected solution that ensures Hub model usage data is efficiently captured, enriched, and stored for reporting and archival purposes. The pipeline begins with Filebeat, a lightweight log shipper that runs as a daemonset alongside our application pods in each Kubernetes cluster. Filebeat's role is to collect logs from various sources, including application containers, and forward them to the next stage of the pipeline.

Once logs are collected by Filebeat, they are sent to Logstash, a powerful log processing tool. Logstash acts as the data processing workhorse, applying a series of mutations and transformations to the incoming logs. This includes enriching logs with GeoIP data for geolocation insights, routing logs to specific Elasticsearch indexes based on predefined criteria, and manipulating log fields by adding, removing, or reformatting them to ensure consistency and ease of analysis. After Logstash has processed the logs, they are forwarded to an Elasticsearch cluster.

In a recent development, elasticsearch, a distributed search and analytics engine, forms the core of our log storage and analysis platform. It receives the logs from Logstash and applies its own set of processing rules through Elasticsearch pipelines. These pipelines perform minimal processing tasks, such as adding timestamp fields to indicate the time of processing, which is crucial for log analysis and correlation. Elasticsearch provides a scalable and flexible storage solution, allowing us to buffer logs for operational use and real-time analysis.

To manage the lifecycle of logs within Elasticsearch, we employ a robust storage and lifecycle management strategy. This ensures that logs are retained in Elasticsearch for a defined period, providing quick access for operational and troubleshooting purposes. After this retention period, logs are offloaded to long-term archival storage. The archival process involves an automated tool that reads logs from Elasticsearch indexes, formats them as Parquet files—an efficient columnar storage format—and writes them to our object storage system.

The final stage of our logging pipeline leverages AWS data warehousing services. Here, AWS Glue crawlers are utilized to discover and classify data in our object storage, automatically generating a Glue Data Catalog, which provides a unified metadata repository. The Glue table schema is periodically refreshed to ensure it remains up-to-date with the evolving structure of our log data. This integration with AWS Glue enables us to query the archived logs using Amazon Athena, a serverless interactive query service. Athena allows us to run SQL queries directly against the data in object storage, providing a cost-effective and scalable solution for log analysis and historical data exploration.

Another point of fragility is the auto-schema detection mechanism in Elasticsearch. While it is designed to adapt to changing log structures, it can fail when application logs undergo significant field type changes. If the schema detection fails to recognize the new field types, it may lead to failed writes from Logstash to Elasticsearch, causing log processing bottlenecks and potential data inconsistencies. This problem highlights the importance of proactive log schema management and the need for robust monitoring to detect and address such issues promptly.

Recent findings suggest that memory management is also a critical aspect of the pipeline's stability. The log processing tier, including Logstash and Filebeat, operates with limited memory resources to control costs. When backpressure occurs, these components can experience Out-of-Memory (OOM) complications, especially during system slowdowns. As logs accumulate and backpressure increases, the memory footprint of these processes grows, pushing them closer to their limits. If not addressed promptly, this can lead to process crashes or further exacerbation of the backpressure problem.

Recent findings suggest that archival jobs, responsible for transferring logs from Elasticsearch to object storage, have also encountered challenges. On occasion, these jobs can be resource-intensive, with their performance becoming sensitive to node size and memory availability. In cases where junk data or unusually large log entries pass through the pipeline, they can strain the archival process, leading to failures due to memory exhaustion or node capacity limits. This underscores the importance of data validation and filtering earlier in the pipeline to prevent such problems from reaching the archival stage.

To mitigate these potential failures, we've implemented a powerful alert system with a unique motivation: validating end-to-end log flow. The alert is designed to compare the number of requests received by our Application Load Balancer (ALB) with the number of logs successfully archived, providing a comprehensive view of log data flow throughout the entire pipeline. This approach allows us to swiftly identify any discrepancies that might indicate potential log loss or processing concerns.

According to recent reports, the alert mechanism is based on a simple yet effective comparison: the number of requests hitting our ALB, which represents the total log volume entering the system, versus the number of logs successfully archived in our long-term storage. By monitoring this ratio, we can ensure that what goes in must come out, providing a robust validation of our logging infrastructure's health. When the alert is triggered, it indicates a potential mismatch, prompting immediate investigation and remediation.

In practice, this alert has proven to be a valuable tool, especially during periods of infrastructure refactoring. For instance, when we migrated our ALB to a VPC origin, the alert was instrumental in identifying and addressing the resulting log flow discrepancies. However, it has also saved us in less obvious scenarios. For example, when archive jobs failed to run due to unforeseen challenges, the alert flagged the missing archived logs, allowing us to promptly investigate and resolve the problem before it impacted our log analysis and retention processes.

Sources indicate that when operating cloud-native applications and Kubernetes-based infrastructures, even seemingly minor problems can escalate into significant downtime if left unchecked. This is particularly true for the Kubernetes API, which serves as the central nervous system of a Kubernetes cluster, orchestrating the creation, management, and networking of containers. At Hugging Face, we've learned through experience that monitoring the Kubernetes API error rate and rate limiting metrics is a crucial practice, one that can prevent potential disasters.

Hugging Face's infrastructure is deeply integrated with Kubernetes, and the kube-rs library has been instrumental in building and managing this ecosystem efficiently. kube-rs offers a Rust-centric approach to Kubernetes application development, providing developers with a familiar and powerful toolkit. At its core, kube-rs introduces three key concepts: reflectors, controllers, and custom resource interfaces. Reflectors ensure real-time synchronization of Kubernetes resources, enabling applications to react swiftly to changes. Controllers, the decision-makers, continuously reconcile the desired and actual states of resources, making Kubernetes self-healing. Custom resource interfaces extend Kubernetes, allowing developers to define application-specific resources for better abstraction.

Additionally, kube-rs introduces watchers and finalizers. Watchers monitor specific resources for changes, triggering actions in response to events. Finalizers, on the other hand, ensure proper cleanup and resource termination by defining custom logic. By providing Rust-based abstractions for these Kubernetes concepts, kube-rs allows developers to build robust, efficient applications, leveraging the Kubernetes platform's power and flexibility while maintaining a Rust-centric development approach. The metric used in this query is container_network_transmit_packets_total, which represents the total number of packets transmitted by a container. The query is filtering for metrics from a cluster’s local Prometheus instance, which is tasked with metric collection as well as remote writing to our central metric store — Grafana Mimir. Transmission of packets approximates healthy remote writes, which is what we want to ensure across all active clusters.

Recent findings suggest that the first part of the query performs a current rate check. The -1 * multiplication is used to invert the result, so that if the historical rate is greater than 0, the result will be less than 0.

Industry observers note that the or operator combines the two parts of the query. The query will return true if either of the following conditions is met:.

According to recent reports, the outer < 0 condition checks if the result of the or operation is less than 0. This means that the query will only trigger if neither of the conditions is met, i.e., if a cluster has never sent any metrics (both current and historical rates are 0).

In both cases, the query will detect that the cluster is not sending any metrics and trigger the alert.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A homelabber detailed improvements to the second-gen Optane AI build in a follow-up post on Reddit, showing the addition of two RTX 3090s to run the 2.8-trillion-parameter Moonshot Kimi K3 model at 3.11 tokens per second.
  • That speed is not the most impressive, but it comes with 16.8 tokens per second for prompt evaluation, with 45 of 94 shards, or 414 GB out of 865 GB, living on a RAM drive.
  • 45 of 94 shards (414 GB of 865 GB) in a tmpfs RAM drive, the rest in Optane.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A homelabber detailed improvements to the second-gen Optane AI build in a follow-up post on Reddit, showing the addition of two RTX 3090s to run the 2.8-trillion-parameter Moonshot Kimi K3 model at 3.11 tokens per second. Transferring almost half the model onto a RAM drive added a significant 41% to generation speed and 26% to prompt evaluation. The extra fans are still needed, though, as the persistent Optane memory gets very hot.

That speed is not the most impressive, but it comes with 16.8 tokens per second for prompt evaluation, with 45 of 94 shards, or 414 GB out of 865 GB, living on a RAM drive. Such an arrangement is not newly introduced to enthusiasts who would set aside system memory for extra-fast performance in a pseudo-non-volatile manner — it’s still volatile, but appears like a disk — although not everyone has that much RAM sitting around free these days. With both GPUs but no RAM drive, the build ran at 2.20 tokens per second for generation and 13.3 for prompt evaluation.

45 of 94 shards (414 GB of 865 GB) in a tmpfs RAM drive, the rest in Optane.

Builder’s measurements; llama.cpp, DAX on for the Optane portion.

Even a quick read of the details makes it clear that the GPUs aren’t holding the model: two RTX 3090s, at 24 GB apiece, only have a total of 48 GB of VRAM, which is about 5.5% of the 865 GB model file. That mentioned, the model is a mixture-of-experts (MoE) type, where its weights are split into multiple “experts” with only a few run per token. Any given token will have “routed” experts selected for it, while “shared” experts run on every token.

It has been revealed that for this model, with 896 experts, 16 are chosen per token, with two shared, with an active 104B parameters out of its 2.8T. All 2.8T parameters would take about 5.6 TB at 16-bit precision. Moonshot’s own release, which uses the 4-bit MXFP4 format, comes to about 1.56 TB, and the Q2_K file used here shrinks that to 865 GB, an average of under 3 bits per parameter. The 865 GB figure is likely in gibibytes (GiB), but for clarity we’re using the GB values as written by the homelabber.

Industry observers note that the configuration here has the routed-expert tensors stay on the CPU side, originally in Optane, and now in Optane plus the RAM drive. The RTX 3090s handle attention, or how each token weighs the rest of the context, and the dense feed-forward network layer that isn’t split into experts, where every token passes through it. They also manage the shared experts, other active-dense components, the KV cache, and the stored context of the current conversation, with the GPU compute buffers. Basically, the parts on the GPUs are “used on every token,” and the improvements there come from the high level of GPU compute and memory bandwidth.

In a recent development, DRAM is a lot slower than VRAM, but it’s still capable of giving a decent speedup. The newly introduced build involves using Linux’s tmpfs, which, per the kernel documentation, “is a file system which keeps all of its files in virtual memory.” Those shards now live in memory, which admittedly is not ideal when the original build was designed to save money by using Optane instead. With those shards in DRAM, which the builder has noted is faster than Optane, that part of the model no longer has to be read from the slower memory; the workload is decidedly distributed.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

In a recent development, the speed that came with the GPUs is within the range of what the builder expected, guessing “somewhere between 2 and 4 tokens per second” in a prediction from the original build thread. The GPU install had to wait, in part, for modifications to the case, which required cutting out some of the metal and relocating the PSU to make room for the GPUs and their cooling. Cooling remains a huge problem, with “the improved throughput [not changing] the original thermal warning,” and the two 12W blower fans for the Optane DIMMs are kept in place. Add in dual 350W-class GPUs, and the changes are understandable.

Things won’t stop here, as more optimizations are possible, including “customized quantization,” which may be similar to the techniques used by lawyer Nick Mermiges. Quantization selected per tensor or layer, or by where the data lives, might reduce bandwidth and capacity pressures for the slower tiers; the setup “might be faster yet.” Speed, or tokens per second alone, is not enough, and output quality must be taken into consideration in any future plan.

  • Industry observers note that small language models are becoming increasingly key as consumers seek capable models that can be deployed efficiently.
  • SmolLM3 sits in the efficiency sweet spot.
  • The complete recipe: We're releasing SmolLM3 with our engineering blueprint.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that small language models are becoming increasingly key as consumers seek capable models that can be deployed efficiently. The community has produced a fascinating range of capable small models, each pushing the boundaries of what's possible at this scale. With SmolLM3, we're excited to contribute a new competitive fully open 3B model:.

SmolLM3 sits in the efficiency sweet spot. Our 3B model outperforms Llama-3.2-3B and Qwen2.5-3B while staying competitive with larger 4B alternatives (Qwen3 & Gemma3). Beyond the performance numbers, we're sharing exactly how we built it using public datasets and training frameworks.

The complete recipe: We're releasing SmolLM3 with our engineering blueprint. It includes architecture details, exact data mixtures showing how we progressively boost performance across domains in a three-stage pretraining approach, and the methodology for building a hybrid reasoning model. Usually, achieving these results would require months of reverse engineering. Instead, we're providing the full methodology.

Whether you're building your own models or want to understand what drives performance at this scale, this blueprint shows the engineering story behind competitive 3B performance.

Let’s have a look at the pretraining stage.

SmolLM3 both changed the architecture and data mixture over its predecessors. Let’s have a look at the architecture and training configurations first!

SmolLM3 follows a transformer decoder architecture with tied embedding similar to SmolLM2, building on Llama architecture with some key modifications optimized for efficiency and long context performance.

Recent findings suggest that grouped Query Attention (GQA): We replaced multi-head attention with grouped-query attention using 4 groups. Our ablations on a 3B model trained with 100B tokens from FineWeb-Edu showed that GQA matches the performance of multi-head attention while significantly reducing the KV cache size during inference.

NoPE: We implemented NoPE from "RoPE to NoRoPE and Back Again: A Newly introduced Hybrid Attention Strategy" (Yang et al., 2025), selectively removing rotary position embeddings from every 4th layer. This approach improves long context performance without affecting short context capabilities, as confirmed by our ablations.

In a recent development, intra-Document Masking: Following "Analysing The Impact of Sequence Composition on Language Model Pre-Training", during training, we use attention masking to ensure tokens from different documents in the same training sequence don't attend to each other. Similar to Llama 3, this helps with faster and more stable long context training while maintaining short context performance.

Training Stability: Following OLMo 2, we remove weight decay from embedding layers to improve training stability. This modification contributed to more stable training dynamics, with embedding norms naturally stabilizing at healthier values during training without impacting overall performance in our ablations.

All these changes were validated through ablations using the same 3B architecture trained on 100B tokens from FineWeb-Edu, ensuring each modification either improved performance or maintained it while offering other benefits.

Industry observers note that training Configuration: We use a global batch size of 2.36M tokens with 4096 sequence length, a learning rate of 2e-4, and the AdamW optimizer (beta1: 0.9, beta2: 0.95) with weight decay of 0.1 and gradient clipping of 1. We use the WSD (Warmup-Stable-Decay) scheduler, with 2000  warmup steps, and a linear decay to 0 in the final 10% training steps. We use nanotron framework for the training, datatrove for data processing and lighteval for evaluation. The model was trained on 384 H100 GPUs for 24 days. You can see the distributed training setup in the following figure.

In addition to architecture changes we also ablated and improved the training recipe. Let’s have a closer look.

Following SmolLM2's multi-stage approach, we train SmolLM3 on 11.2T tokens using a three-stage training strategy that mixes web, math, and code data with evolving proportions. We conducted extensive ablations on 3B models trained on 50B to 100B tokens to determine the data mixture and ratios.

The pretraining consists of these stages, also shown in the figure above:.

According to recent reports, with these stages and mixtures we achieved very competitive performance for the base model. More on that in the evaluation section. The nanotron training configs with exact data weights can be found here. We will also share our training logs along with intermediate checkpoints.

After the main pretraining we improved the model in a mid-training stage for long context and reasoning.

According to recent reports, we call the long context adaptation and reasoning adaptation “mid-training”. They are much shorter than the main pretraining but still somewhat general and aimed at improving the model in those two domains. Let’s first have a look at long context training.

After the main pretraining, we trained SmolLM3 on an additional 100B tokens to extend its context length. We sequentially extended the context window in two stages for 50B tokens each: first transitioning from 4k to 32k context with RoPE theta increased to 1.5M, then from 32k to 64k context with RoPE theta increased to 5M. Both stages upsampled math, code, and reasoning data. During ablations, we found that upsampling specific long context data such as code repositories, books, and long web pages (beyond the naturally long samples in our mixture) didn't further boost performance on RULER and HELMET benchmarks. Using NoPE and training on the decay mixture with longer sequences and increased RoPE theta values was sufficient to achieve competitive long context performance up to 64k.

Following Qwen2.5, we use YARN to extrapolate beyond the training context length. During inference, the model can handle up to  128k context (2x extension beyond the 64k training length).

Sources indicate that after extending the context length of the model, we trained it at a mid-training stage to incorporate reasoning capabilities. The main difference between the mid-training stage and the pre- and post-training stages is that we targeted a general capability without yet focusing on a specific domain. In our case, we wanted to train the model to reason without targeting a particular domain, such as mathematics or computer code.

Sources indicate that our mid-training dataset contained 35B tokens sourced from Open Thought’s OpenThoughts3-1.2M and a subset from NVIDIA’s Llama-Nemotron-Post-Training-Dataset-v1.1 with reasoning traces from R1. We used the ChatML chat template and wrapped packing to avoid providing too much structure to the model. We trained the model for 4 (~140B tokens) epochs and used the checkpoint for subsequent SFT stages.

The release of reasoning models like DeepSeek R1 and Qwen3 has demonstrated the powerful capabilities that emerge when models can engage in explicit reasoning. However, the community still lacks fully open recipes with public datasets to build dual instruction models that support both reasoning and non-reasoning modes. Most existing approaches involve complex reinforcement learning processes and proprietary datasets, making it difficult for researchers to reproduce and build upon these results.

In a recent development, in this section, we explain how we tackled these challenges and share our complete recipe for building a dual instruction model. We detail how we balance performance between reasoning and non-reasoning modes through a carefully designed training pipeline that includes mid-training for general reasoning capabilities, supervised fine-tuning with synthetic data generation, and alignment using Anchored Preference Optimization (APO) - a recent variant of DPO.

Before diving into the training methodology, it's essential to establish how consumers interact with our dual-mode model. The chat template serves as the interface that enables seamless switching between reasoning and non-reasoning modes, and its design directly impacts both our training data format and model behavior. SmolLM3's chat template allows users to control the reasoning mode during a conversation. Users can activate reasoning or non-reasoning modes by including the /think and /no_think flags, respectively, in the system prompt. In non-reasoning mode, we pre-fill the model's response with empty think blocks, similar to Qwen3, to ensure direct answers without explicit reasoning.

Industry observers note that smolLM3 supports tool calling, and its chat template incorporates two distinct sections for tool descriptions: XML Tools and Python Tools. This specific categorization proved beneficial in our experiments for the model's accurate interpretation of tool definitions in each format.

Sources indicate that the chat template provides a default system message for both reasoning modes, along with a metadata section that includes the date, knowledge cut-off date, and current reasoning mode. Users can replace the default system message by providing one with the system role. The metadata section can be excluded by using the /system_override flag in the system prompt, offering flexibility for specific use cases.

Following the reasoning mid-training stage, where we trained the model on 140B tokens of general reasoning data, we proceed with Supervised Finetuning (SFT) to incorporate capabilities across both reasoning and non-reasoning modes for math, code, general reasoning, instruction following, multilinguality, and tool calling. Training a dual-mode model requires carefully balancing the data mixture to maintain strong performance in both modes across all target domains. To evaluate SmolLM3’s performance throughout training, we tracked the following domains: math, code, general reasoning, instruction following, and multilinguality.

The primary challenge we encountered when building the reasoning mode dataset was the scarcity of datasets containing reasoning traces for certain domains. To address this gap, we generated synthetic data by prompting Qwen3-32B in reasoning mode with prompts from existing non-reasoning datasets. This allowed us to improve performance in domains where the model initially struggled in reasoning mode, such as multi-turn conversations, multilinguality, and everyday conversations.

Our final data mixture was the result of extensive ablations examining the optimal ratio of reasoning to non-reasoning tokens and the composition within each mode. The resulting SFT dataset contains 1.8B tokens: 1B in non-reasoning mode and 0.8B in reasoning mode, comprising 12 non-reasoning datasets and 10 datasets with reasoning traces. We trained for 4 epochs (~8B tokens) using BFD (best-fit decreasing) packing with the loss masked on user turns and the results from tool calls.

We will release this data mixture along with our full training scripts to enable the community to reproduce and build upon our work.

After the SFT step, we performed a round of model alignment using a combination of the Tulu3 preference dataset for non-reasoning mode and newly introduced synthetic preference pairs for reasoning mode, that we generated from Qwen3-32B and Qwen3-0.6B. To ensure full coverage of all domains in the non-thinking dataset, we generated complementing thinking mode preference pairs. We selected generations from Qwen3-32B as “chosen” and responses from Qwen3-0.6B as “rejected” for alignment with Anchored Preference Optimization.

It has been revealed that anchored Preference Optimization (APO) is a variant of Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) that provides a more stable optimization objective. In DPO, the reward function r_θ(x,y) measures the log-ratio of the probability of the sequence during training compared to the model at the start of training, the reference model:.

Recent findings suggest that here β controls how much the model being optimized can change relative to the reference model. The DPO loss optimizes triplets of prompts x, chosen y_w and rejected y_l responses:.

The APO objective has been shown to be more stable, and we also observed higher downstream performance in our internal ablations.

Sources indicate that while downstream evaluations demonstrated improvements across mathematics, science, instruction following, coding, chat, and multilingual tasks, we observed performance degradation on long context benchmarks like RULER. We traced this degradation back to the reasoning mid-training stage, where the focus on reasoning capabilities impacted long context performance. Additionally, the APO training data was limited to 24k tokens since the vast majority of our reasoning dataset fell below this length.

To mitigate this performance drop, we explored model merging as a solution.

Industry observers note that model merging is a popular and powerful technique that allows combining the strengths of different models without the computational overhead of ensembling or the need for additional training. We used the MergeKit library to perform the model merging, as it includes several merging methods, including linear and non-linear merging.

Our merging recipe consists of two steps:.

Industry observers note that the resulting model is the checkpoint we are releasing today. It maintains performance across a wide range of tasks. So let’s turn to the evaluation result both of this model as well as the base model.

We evaluate base models and the instruct model both in reasoning and non-reasoning mode. Let’s first cover the base model’s performance!

The plot below demonstrates SmolLM3's win rate across 12 popular benchmarks evaluating knowledge, reasoning, math, and coding capabilities. SmolLM3 consistently outperforms other 3B models and achieves competitive performance with larger 4B models including Qwen3-4B and Gemma3-4B.

Evaluation benchmarks used for the win rate: HellaSwag, ARC, Winogrande, CommonsenseQA, MMLU-CF, MMLU Pro CF, PIQA, OpenBookQA, GSM8K, MATH, HumanEval+, MBPP+.

SmolLM3 achieves first or second place on knowledge and reasoning benchmarks (HellaSwag, ARC, BoolQ), demonstrating strong performance in these core capabilities. Math and coding performance is competitive within the 3B class. Long-context performance on Ruler 64k shows the model can handle extended sequences effectively.

In a recent development, the model demonstrates strong multilingual performance across five major European languages when evaluated on multilingual benchmarks including Global MMLU, MLMM HellaSwag, Flores-200, Belebele, testing knowledge, commonsense reasoning, text understanding, and translation. This indicates SmolLM3 maintains consistent performance beyond English.

It has been revealed that in summary, the base model indicates very strong performance across many domains. Let’s see how this translates to the instruct model’s performance.

Since SmolLM3 has both an instruct and reasoning mode we need to evaluate the model in both modes and compare to models with same capabilities.

We evaluate SmolLM3 against other 3B non-reasoning models and compare it to Qwen3 reasoning models in no thinking mode across multiple benchmarks. As shown in the performance chart, SmolLM3 outperforms other 3B non-reasoning models including Llama3.2 3B Instruct and Qwen2.5 3B Instruct and sits at an efficiency sweet spot between reasoning models, significantly outperforming Qwen3 1.7B while getting close to the 4B model performance at a lower computational cost.

So the instruct model sits right at the pareto front of performance and cost. Let’s see how the reasoning model does!

It has been revealed that when evaluating SmolLM3's reasoning capabilities with extended thinking enabled, the model reveals substantial improvements across most benchmarks compared to its non-reasoning counterpart. We observe notable gains in challenging tasks like AIME 2025 (36.7% vs 9.3%), competitive programming on LiveCodeBench (30.0% vs 15.2%), and graduate-level reasoning on GPQA Diamond (41.7% vs 35.7%).

Industry observers note that while Qwen3 4B generally achieves the highest scores across both thinking and non-thinking modes, SmolLM3 demonstrates competitive performance within the 3B parameter class, particularly excelling in mathematical reasoning and complex problem-solving tasks. The model's dual-mode capability allows customers to choose between faster inference without reasoning or more thorough analysis with extended thinking.

So the last question is: how can you use the model?

Recent findings suggest that the modeling code for SmolLM3 is available in transformers v4.53.0, so make sure to upgrade your transformers version. You can also load the model with the latest vllm which uses transformers as a backend.

We recommend setting temperature=0.6 and top_p=0.95 in the sampling parameters.

Industry observers note that we enable extended thinking by default, so the example above generates the output with a reasoning trace. For choosing between enabling, you can provide the /think and /no_think flags through the system prompt as shown in the snippet below for extended thinking disabled. The code for generating the response with extended thinking would be the same except that the system prompt should have /think instead of /no_think.

SmolLM3 supports tool calling! Just pass your list of tools under the argument xml_tools (for standard tool-calling), or python_tools (for calling tools like python functions in a  snippet).

We release SmolLM3, a small, long-context, multilingual, reasoner with up to 128k context. In addition to the model checkpoint we release the full training recipe including pre-training, mid-training, post-training, and synthetic data generation as well as the datasets (coming shortly). We hope this model proves useful to the community and the recipe will allow other groups to improve upon it.

According to recent reports, your focus on pushing the boundaries of long-context performance is fascinating. It reminded me of a recent paper that tackles the same challenge from a completely different architectural angle.

I was just reading about ATLAS from Google Research (arXiv:2505.23735), which proposes replacing the standard attention mechanism with a modern recurrent "long-term memory module".

Sources indicate that the core idea is to overcome the limitations of both Transformers and older RNNs by creating a memory that explicitly "learns to memorize the context" instead of just individual tokens. They introduce a concept called the Omega Rule, which updates the memory based on a sliding window of the past, rather than the "online" token-by-token enhancement that can lead to complications like the "lost in the middle" problem.

The results they show are compelling, especially its ability to scale effectively to a 10M context length on the BABILong benchmark.

Recent findings suggest that it's exciting to see two powerful—and very different—approaches for scaling context length. One path is perfecting the Transformer architecture (like SmolLM3), and the other is designing upcoming memory-centric recurrent models (like ATLAS).

In a recent development, we use a vocabulary with 128K tokens. Our token vocabulary combines 100K tokens from the tiktoken3tokenizer with 28K additional tokens to better support non-English languages. Compared to the Llama2 tokenizer, our latest tokenizer improves compression rates on a sample of English data from 3.17 to3.94 characters per token. This enables the model to “read” more text for the same amount of trainingcompute. We also found that adding 28K tokens from select non-English languages improved bothcompression ratios and downstream performance, with no impact on English tokenization.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every developer has shipped the other kind of page: a lovingly written article or landing page that peaks on launch day and then quietly rots. Screenshots age, statistics expire, rankings slide. Data-driven pages play the opposite game. Built from a living dataset, they republish themselves daily, grow to thousands of URLs, and answer questions nobody had asked when the site launched. This guide breaks down how they work, using a real fan-run stats site as the running example: one public dataset in, more than ten thousand fresh pages out.

In a recent development, static pages lose ground because the web moves and they do not. Facts expire, competitors publish fresher answers, and search engines reward pages whose information matches today. A page that cannot enhancement itself must be rewritten by hand, so most sites update a few pages and abandon the rest.

In a recent development, freshness is not one rule for the whole web; it depends on the query. Nobody needs a CSS tutorial rewritten weekly, but statistics, prices, availability and anything with a season attached decays on a schedule. Developers misjudge this constantly, treating every page like documentation when half their catalogue is really a perishable good. Serve a three-month-old stat as if it were current and readers learn the most damaging lesson a site can teach: do not trust the numbers here.

Then there is the maintenance maths. A hundred hand-written pages each needing one review a year is a hundred small debts, and the interest compounds as the catalogue grows. The team updates the flagship pages, promises to return for the rest, and quietly never does. Data-driven architecture is really a staffing decision disguised as a technical one: humans design the system once, and the system does the updating forever.

According to recent reports, A data-driven site has three layers: a dataset that refreshes on a schedule, templates that turn records into pages, and URL patterns that map every meaningful combination people might search for. Change the data and every page changes; improve a template and ten thousand pages improve at once.

The running example makes this concrete. A fan-built Overwatch stats tracker republishes Blizzard's public hero data on a daily cycle. From that one feed it generates hero profiles, head-to-head matchup pages and multi-condition tier lists: 10,291 URLs in its sitemap, across six languages, with matchup pages alone accounting for 8,586 of them. Nobody wrote those pages. Somebody designed the system that writes them, which is a very different, and much more scalable, job.

In a recent development, the example runs on Next.js behind a CDN, but the stack is the least important layer of the three. The same pipeline feeding WordPress, Astro or a static site generator would look identical from the reader's side of the glass. Choose boring technology you already know, and spend your originality budget on the dataset and the templates, because that is where readers will feel the difference.

In a recent development, generated pages stay useful when every URL must earn its existence with data. Set minimum thresholds before a page is published, give each template unique modules its siblings do not have, and noindex combinations with nothing to say. The line between a resource and spam is not automation; it is emptiness.

Quality gates work best when they are public and mechanical. The example site publishes its tier formula openly: 70% of the score from win rate, 30% from pick rate, and a hard floor that excludes heroes picked in under 0.5% of matches from topping the ranking, because a tiny sample cannot prove anything. That single floor is editorial policy expressed as code. Your version might be a minimum number of data points, a minimum price history, or a minimum review count — the number matters less than the fact that the gate exists and applies to every page equally.

Each template also needs modules its siblings cannot copy. A hero profile carries a seven-day trend and its best and worst matchups; a matchup page carries the head-to-head history; a tier list carries the movement since yesterday. Add a short human layer on top — a methodology page explaining the scoring, changelogs narrating what moved — and the catalogue stops reading as output and starts reading as a publication. Google's scaled-content rules target pages manufactured to manipulate rankings with little value; a page that answers a real query with real, current data is the opposite of that. The honest test for any generated URL is simple: if it vanished tonight, would a searcher lose an answer?

Start embarrassingly small: one dataset, one entity type, one template. A football club's results archive, a property portal's sold prices, your own product catalogue — anything structured and refreshed beats a grand initiative. Prove one template earns traffic, then add combinations, languages and dashboards in that order.

Industry observers note that what is programmatic SEO? Programmatic SEO means generating many pages from a structured dataset using templates, instead of writing each page by hand. Done well, each page answers a distinct search with real data. Done badly, it produces thousands of near-identical pages, which is where its reputation suffers.

Recent findings suggest that is programmatic SEO against Google's rules? No. Google's spam policies target scaled content created mainly to manipulate rankings, with little or no value for owners. Pages generated from real data that answer real queries are publishing. The deciding question is whether a page helps its reader, not how it was produced.

In a recent development, how often should the data behind pages refresh? Match the refresh to how fast the underlying facts change. Sports and game statistics justify daily pulls, prices often need hourly checks, and reference data may only move monthly. Refreshing faster than reality changes wastes crawl budget and makes 'updated' stamps meaningless.

Sources indicate that do generated pages need unique written text? They need unique value, which is not the same thing. Identical paragraphs on ten thousand pages add nothing, but unique data, comparisons and trends are content in their own right. Add short human-written context per template, and let the data carry the differences between pages.

Sources indicate that how many pages should a first project launch with? Launch with the smallest set that proves the template: one entity type, a few hundred pages at most. Validate that search engines index them and people engage before adding combinations and languages. Scaling an unproven template just manufactures tomorrow's cleanup job at industrial size.

The sites quietly winning the long game are not publishing more; they are publishing systems. One honest dataset, one well-built template and strict quality gates will outlast a hundred hand-written pages competing on freshness alone. Try it this week: take one dataset you already own, design a single template with four real modules, and ship fifty pages. Watch what the data does next.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Phones have gotten a lot more expensive over the last year or so, and it’s a trend we’re expecting to get worse before it can get better.
  • While buying year-old hardware typically comes with some pretty deep sacrifices between generations, that’s not particularly true with the Pixel 10 this year.
  • So what are you giving up that matters?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Phones have gotten a lot more expensive over the last year or so, and it’s a trend we’re expecting to get worse before it can get better. If you’re in the market for an upgrade, this year’s Black Friday might be one of the final truly good times to buy a upcoming device, and for just $600, last year’s Pixel 10 should be high on your list.

While buying year-old hardware typically comes with some pretty deep sacrifices between generations, that’s not particularly true with the Pixel 10 this year. From a hardware perspective, nearly everything is either identical or close enough to not particularly matter. Its design and display are all but unchanged, Qi2-ready magnets come on both models, and both devices are built with the same level of battery longevity in mind. And much to the chagrin of many a Pixel die-hard, Tensor G5 and Tensor G6 are practically interchangeable.

So what are you giving up that matters? When the Pixel 11 arrived, software features made up the bulk of this list, but with last week’s Pixel Drop, a lot of the gaps between these two generations have been closed. Gemini Intelligence with Rambler, app automation, and more are in the process of rolling out to existing Pixel 10 owners, and latest features like Create My Widget arrived on the Pixel 10 and 11 at the exact same time. From a software perspective — Google’s bread and butter, in my eyes — the only major sacrifice comes from the year of software support that’s already complete, leaving you with just six instead of seven.

Realistically, the camera is the one place you’re likely to feel a difference. The Pixel 10 was the first non-Pro device in Google’s Tensor era to ship with a telephoto lens, but it came with some significant sacrifices. The main sensor is effectively an A-series lens, and taken together, the entire package might leave something to be desired. It’s far from a bad camera though — I used it as my main shooter through most of its lifecycle — and while the Pixel 11 did get some upgrades here, I think real shutterbugs would be better off looking at Google’s Pro lineup anyway. You’ll also lose out on things like HiLight, though really, are you missing that much?

Sources indicate that what makes this deal so good is really its place in the market, not as a direct comparison to the newer Pixel 11. For $600, Google’s competition is going to have a hard time competing with the value the Pixel 10 delivers. Hell, even Google might find it difficult to compete in the coming months; at full price, $600 is what the Pixel 10a goes for now, a decidedly less-impressive device compared to this model. No, this is a flagship smartphone through and through, and for $600, you’re effectively guaranteeing a reliable, powerful smartphone experience from now until 2032 — hopefully enough time for this whole RAM crisis to finally simmer down a bit.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Honor Watch 6 Pro has a 5,500-nit OLED display, ceramic bezel, 18-day battery life, and costs less than it looks.

In a recent development, in the world of athletic smartwatches, it isn’t often that you could mistake one for a luxury watch, but Honor seems to want to flip all that on its head with the Honor Watch 6 Pro. Just take a look at this excerpt from the firm’s press release:.

Framing this brilliant display is a Precision Nanocrystalline Ceramic bezel crafted through a 1400°C high-temperature integrated sintering process, delivering a delicate texture and rich visual depth.

Inspired by modernist architecture, its diamond-cut octagonal rotatable crown features a dual-layer horizontal and vertical cut, complemented by a side button for intuitive navigation.

That sounds pretty wild to me, and it’s backed up by specs that sound just as legit, too. On top is a 1.5-inch LTPO Tandem AMOLED display that outputs 5,500-nit peak brightness. Underneath is a bevy of fresh sensors called the Intelligent Sense System, which Honor indicates combines “multi-wavelength monitoring, multi-optical path patrol technology, and anti-interference glass technology to reach deep skin layers.”.

Recent findings suggest that runners will be pleased to know that the Honor Watch 6 Pro not only incorporates a dual-band GPS, but combines it with a “star-pointing 3-antenna design” and an AI fusion algorithm, which should deliver ultra-accurate tracking in any location and no matter how you hold your wrist. Despite its luxury looks, this one tracks over 120 sports modes, including Honor’s Professional Running Coach feature, which tracks running posture, lactate threshold, heart rate targets, and keeps you on pace with real-time voice coaching.

During sports modes like Badminton, the watch can identify more than six types of swings, and Honor says other sports modes can deliver similarly detailed statistics. The watch is 5ATM, IP68, IP69, and IP69K water-and-dust-resistant rated, plus it integrates directly with Strava so you can pull all your fitness data together.

Sources indicate that honor is incorporating a new wrist twist gesture system this time around, letting you use gestures to perform actions hands-free. The watch is rated at 10 days of battery life on a single charge in regular usage mode, while endurance mode will stretch that to 18 days. Pre-sales begin today, November 19, and run until December 31, when the watch is expected to launch, starting at €279/£229 for early bird pricing. After launch, the retail MSRP starts at €379/£329.

Recent findings suggest that the Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard that enables developers to build secure, two-way connections between an LLM and a set of tools. For example, if you create an MCP server that exposes a tool capable of transcribing a video, then you can connect an LLM client (such as Cursor, Claude Code, or Cline) to the server. The LLM will then know how to transcribe videos and use this tool for you depending on your request.

In short, an MCP server is a standard way to upskill your LLM by granting it a new ability. Think of it like the apps on your smartphone. On its own, your smartphone can't edit images, but you can download an app to do this from the app store. Now, if only there were an app store for MCP servers? 🤔.

That means that Hugging Face Spaces is the one place where you can find thousands of AI-powered abilities for your LLM, aka the MCP App Store!

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, drones have become a major menace on modern battlefields, which is why Turkish defense firm Aselsan has developed a potent solution to counter them.
  • While drones and uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs) have been around for decades now, Russia’s 2022 escalation in Ukraine saw the first widespread use of small drones on the front line, some of which have been adapted from commercial models.
  • Recent findings suggest that many countries have started working on anti-drone defenses, too.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, drones have become a major menace on modern battlefields, which is why Turkish defense firm Aselsan has developed a potent solution to counter them. The company shared a YouTube video showing its Ejderha, which translates to “Dragon” in English Anti-Drone Countermeasure System taking down 51 drones simultaneously. The firm indicates that the device uses high-power electromagnetic (HPEM) waves and vacuum electronics to disable the electronic components on mini and micro drones.

While drones and uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs) have been around for decades now, Russia’s 2022 escalation in Ukraine saw the first widespread use of small drones on the front line, some of which have been adapted from commercial models. Because of this, we’ve seen various innovations in drone technologies, including the deployment of fiber optic drones to defeat radio jamming, the use of an onboard camera looking at a magnetic compass as a backup for GPS navigation, as well as the introduction of jam-resistant strike drones and “flying modems” that relay signals from one drone to another to extend their strike range.

Recent findings suggest that many countries have started working on anti-drone defenses, too. Ukraine has erected mobile barriers with rotating barbed wire designed to cut the fiber-optic lines that jam-proof Russian drones rely on, while various companies in the U.S.—from established players like Lockheed Martin and Northrop Grumman to startups like Mara—have been working on both airborne and ground-based solutions. China has also unveiled a man-portable design that neutralizes drones in under four seconds at up to 1,600 feet away using a 2-kilowatt laser.

Before the invention of the transistor in 1947, electronic devices relied on vacuum tubes, which were invented in 1904 by British engineer John Ambrose Fleming. Today, most devices rely on semiconductors for their power efficiency, reliability, and computing density. But if you need to produce a microwave signal strong enough to overwhelm the electronic components inside a drone, vacuum electronics is still one of the most effective solutions (although some companies are experimenting with solid-state semiconductors, too). The U.S. and the UK are also working on their own HPEM systems, with the former testing the Leonidas Autonomous Ground Vehicle (AGV) and the latter trialing the Radio Frequency Directed Energy Weapon (RFDEW).

A page can return 200 OK, exist in an XML sitemap, and still be practically invisible to anyone browsing the site.

That is the orphan-page problem.

You do not need a full commercial crawler to find the obvious cases. A small Node.js script can compare two things:.

URLs reachable through HTML links.

Anything present in the first set but missing from the second deserves investigation.

Install Cheerio and an XML parser:.

You now have URLs that the application publishes through its sitemap but that your HTML crawl could not reach.

A mismatch is evidence, not a verdict.

The page might be intentionally isolated. It might exist for a campaign. Navigation might depend on JavaScript. Your crawler may have missed authentication or pagination.

Should a normal visitor reasonably be able to discover this page from another page on the site?

If yes, investigate the navigation.

That is also good web architecture independent of SEO.

Internal links should not exist merely to move ranking signals around.

They should help people move between related tasks.

Recent findings suggest that A technical guide might lead to a product page. A product page might link back to the configuration guide. A category page should make crucial child resources discoverable without requiring a user to know the exact URL.

Industry observers note that this is why on-page SEO and internal linking are closely connected to site architecture. Good internal links clarify relationships for both visitors and crawlers.

Industry observers note that at a broader level, crawlability is one part of technical SEO and search visibility. A page that nobody can reliably discover is difficult to evaluate regardless of how strong its content may be.

This crawler reads the HTML response.

If an important URL appears disconnected because navigation is created only after client-side JavaScript runs, the script has surfaced a real architectural fact.

You can then decide whether that is acceptable.

If your application genuinely requires rendered-DOM crawling, replace the fetch-and-Cheerio layer with Playwright.

Do not make the simple crawler pretend to be something it is not.

The best output from this tool is not an "SEO score.".
