📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that more than a billion per day: that’s a low estimate of how many requests ChatGPT handles daily, a number which is unlikely to go down soon. For each request and each generated token, we run an inference of a multi-billion parameters model. This is why model optimization is paramount at each and every level: when one deals with these kinds of scale, even a 1% latency or power gain can bring huge savings.

Industry observers note that but where might that gain come from? Model architectures are already well established, and popular models have had quantized weight for a long time now. However, a crucial level at which we can optimize model inference remains: the kernel level. Kernels are the algorithms executed when you do any operation in your network: there are matrix multiplication kernels, convolution kernels, batch normalization kernels, etc. Kernels are low-level, highly-optimized algorithms, often tailored for the device they will be running on. They are notoriously long and hard to write, and require a good understanding of the inner working of the GPU.

Sources indicate that kernels are essential for running operations in neural networks—without a kernel, an operation effectively can't be used. Because of this, upcoming innovations often launch with a "day 0" kernel, typically optimized only for the latest Nvidia hardware. This approach excludes many other devices, particularly AMD GPUs, which, despite offering comparable or superior specs, are often overlooked by kernel developers. Hugging Face collaborated with AMD to deliver state-of-the-art performance on AMD platforms and make it benefit the open source community. As part of this partnership, we decided with AMD to focus on delivering open-source optimized kernels to improve the performance of serving Llama 3.1 405B in FP8 on a node of 8 MI300X using VLLM.

In this blog post, we'll explore how we optimized performance for the MI300X and how each kernel was individually fine-tuned. But first, let’s look at the performance gains achieved using our custom kernels. By combining the following three optimized kernels:.

we achieved significant speedups when running VLLM on a node powered by MI300X GPUs.

It has been revealed that measures were taken with input size 1 and output size 128 to mimic decoding regime. We measure decoding latency using the median over 30 iterations.

Those performance gains were measured in VLLM, but you may also use the kernels separately, as described in the “How to” section that follows.

Sources indicate that all kernels described previously are available on the hf-rocm-kernels repository located here. In it, you will find instructions on how to install the package, the source code for each kernels, their respective python bindings, various benchmarking scripts and a test suite. Using benchmarking scripts and a MI300X, you may even reproduce from this blog post. To ensure same results for Torch or VLLM, you can use the same container as we did. You can also use the repo as a base to build your own kernels: it has instructions on how to bind a CUDA-style kernel to python and a simple sample kernel. You may even have a look at branches under development for latest kernels, like a compute-and-communicate kernel as described here.

The kernels described will soon be integrated in the AMD fork of the VLLM project, but if you want to have a look at how you might do something like that yourself, you may check out this branch and this document.

In a recent development, we are first going to do a quick refresher on the architecture of the device we are working on: the MI300X. Then, we are going to take a look at the state of our model’s inference before optimizing it. This will allow us to identify bottlenecks and know which custom kernels we need to write. Then, we will take a look at each kernel we have written, which will give us an opportunity to explore how kernel optimization is conducted through many angles.

Sources indicate that before we dive into optimizing GPU code, we need to know how a GPU works. There are a lot of resources out there that already do a great job of explaining the inner workings of your GPU, which I will link right here, here and here. We are still going to run through the different levels of the GPU, as a quick refresher. If you want to skip the refresher and get directly into the details of our custom kernels, click here!

The smallest unit of work in the GPU is the thread. Any time any work is done on a GPU, it’s because a thread executed an instruction. Instructions are basic operations like additions, multiplication, conversion from one data type to another, or loads and stores. Each thread has its own memory, called registers (or VGPRs), which only it can access. A thread can have a maximum of 256 registers, each 32-bit wide. Below is represented a thread with access to its 256 VGPRs.

Threads, except when using load or store instructions, can only execute instructions on their own registers. For instance, to add two vectors A and B together, each thread is going to 1) load in its registers an element from A and 2) another from B, then 3) perform the addition and store the result in another register, and finally 4) store the value from that register in memory. That’s a total of 4 instructions.

It has been revealed that the next unit of work is a warp: each warp is composed of 64 threads. Warps don’t have their own memory, but they are of interest to us because all threads in a warp must execute the same instruction at the same time. This is both a guarantee and a constraint.

It has been revealed that warps also allow for different threads to exchange information coming from their registers with other threads in the same warp. Although different threads in a warp have access to different data, the fact that they all have to execute the same instructions means that when writing a kernel, warp-level behavior is what you need to think about.

Warps are bundled together into thread blocks: thread blocks are software abstractions, but run on a hardware component called a compute unit (CU). A single compute unit can run multiple thread blocks at once, but it can only fit 16 warps. Each compute unit has a dedicated L1 cache and shared memory. L1 cache cannot be controlled or allocated and helps with data reuse of all warps situated on the CU. Conversely, shared memory can be allocated and used as a storage shared by all warps. For instance, when we want all warps (and thus threads) in a compute unit to access the same buffer, we allocate it in shared memory. Both shared memory and L1 cache are fast to access because they are “close” to the threads.

Industry observers note that thread blocks also offer the ability to synchronize all threads running inside: this is quite useful when dealing with operations that impact shared memory, like initializing an array in shared memory to zero or reduction operations. In general, when writing a kernel, thread blocks are the highest level to take into consideration: it’s very hard to synchronize different thread blocks or make them interact in any way whatsoever. Kernel throughput is tightly linked to the number of compute unit present on the GPU: the more CUs there are, the more thread blocks can be run at the same time, which increases throughput if you manage to use all CUs.

Compute units are then grouped into accelerator complex dies (XCDs), which hold 38 compute units each. Although CUs may not interact with each others, they all share a L2 cache which you can’t control but still may prove useful when re-using data. For instance, when accessing memory, having two compute units located on the same XCD access the same data will reduce loading latency by a lot. L2 cache is quite large: it has a size of 4MB, while shared memory has a size of 64kB and L1 cache contains 32kB.

By assembling 8 XCDs (which gives us 8 * 38 = 304 CUs) and adding a last level of cache (called infinity cache, with 256MB) and a huge quantity of video ram (192GB) we get the MI300X.

All XCDs, and thus all threads, have access to the VRAM, but getting there is quite slow. As you get further away from thread-level, memory becomes slower to access but has a larger size and larger scope, meaning it serves more threads. When optimizing a kernel, there is always a balance to strike between doing lots of operations or loading lots of data, but in general, you want to access the VRAM (commonly referred to as global memory) as little as possible.

When looking at this figure, we can see why GPUs are referred to as “massively parallel”: here, we have 304 compute units, which can each run 16 warps, each with 64 threads. This means that we can have up to 311296 threads running at the same time, each executing an instruction of its own. Keep in mind an instruction is something basic like an addition, so simple routines like Newton’s method can be quite long to run for a single thread. GPUs are not optimized for instructions to run fast, i.e. for the latency of each instruction to be low: that would be a latency-oriented device. They are optimized for many threads to be run together, consuming and outputting a large quantity of data: it is a throughput-oriented device. When optimizing a kernel for the GPU, we adapt in consequence: it is better to have an algorithm running a few instructions on many threads at once, than having it run many instructions on a few threads. Hence calling algorithms running on GPUs “parallel”.

What can get in the way of such algorithms running in an optimized manner are three things: when there is a lot of data to load (memory bound), when there are many operations to performs (compute bound) or when threads have to work together (synchronization overhead).

When optimizing a workload, the first thing to do before writing a single line of code is to profile the current state of the workload. In our case, we are going to profile the model inference in VLLM to get an idea of how much time each operation is taking up. This can help identify major bottlenecks and which kernels we can tackle first for maximum speedup. For instance, here is the breakdown for batch size 32:.

We can see the different parts of the network through each slice:.

Recent findings suggest that already we can see that most of the latency comes from GEMMs and communications, but also that attention and the operations surrounding it are not a major contributor to latency. This can come as a surprise, because a lot of papers focus on attention and reducing its cost, but it seems that through a combination of KV caching and FlashAttention, which has already been optimized in VLLM, this part may no longer be a top priority. Surprisingly, the two calls made to the “RMS norm” kernel are quite costly, so there might be a large benefit to optimizing that kernel. Along with the SwiGLU kernel, they represent 15% of the total latency, which is not negligible. All in all, working on those two kernels, plus trying to gain a small speedup on GEMMs may be our best course of action. To check that this performance breakdown is not a fluke, we can take a look at other batch sizes:.

We can see the pattern that emerged for batch size 32 holds up for other batch sizes, albeit with the latency contribution of GEMMs and communications becoming greater as the batch size increases. Also, it seems that batch size 32 is an outlier when it comes to the latency of GEMMs: it’s probably because the GEMMs chosen when batch size is 32 have been manually tuned or because batch size 32 presents good memory alignment patterns, so GEMMs for batch size 32 are faster than for batch size 24 or 28.

Now that we have identified some hot spots to optimize, let’s take a look at the first kernel we wrote: the RMS norm kernel.

In each decoder block, we have two main parts: an attention block and an MLP block. Both begin with a residual connection between two inputs: the current hidden states x x x and the residual r r r . Both have the same shape, which is n n n rows (as many as there are tokens) and d d d columns. After they are added together, we apply a row-wise Root Mean Square (RMS) norm to x x x and, since the model is in FP8, we quantize x x x to FP8 using a scale s s s . Simply fusing those three operations into a single kernel can deliver a nice performance boost. Mathematically, the operations we have to perform are the following:.

i+j+kx←x+rr←xV=∑i=1dxi2x←xV+ϵxQ=Qfp8(s∗x∗w) \begin{align} \phantom{i + j + k} &\begin{aligned} x &\leftarrow x + r\\ r &\leftarrow x \end{aligned}\\ &\begin{aligned} V &= \sum_{i=1}^{d} x_i^2 \end{aligned}\\ &\begin{aligned} x &\leftarrow \frac{x}{\sqrt{V + \epsilon}} \\ x_Q &= Q_{\text{fp8}} \left( s * x * w\right) \end{aligned} \end{align} i+j+k​xr​←x+r←x​V​=i=1∑d​xi2​​xxQ​​←V+ϵ​x​=Qfp8​(s∗x∗w)​​​.

It has been revealed that where w w w is a d d d -sized weight vector. Steps (1) and (3) are pretty basic. For step (1), we just need to position each thread to a different location in the tensor, load some elements of x x x and r r r , add them and store back r r r . For step (3), each thread performs some scalar operations (addition, square root, division) and a conversion to FP8. All of this, each thread can do on its own: this is perfectly suited to the parallel nature of the GPU. The step to watch out for is (2): we need to sum over d d d , which means either each thread is going to visit each of the d d d columns, or we need to exchange data between threads. The greater d d d is, the more data we would have to load for the first option, so the less viable it becomes. We are going to pick the second option: synchronize threads at the block level, and they will exchange data using the shared memory. Each thread is going to accumulate a part of V V V on its own and then we are going to sum all of those parts across the thread block, which is what we call a reduction. Since V V V is computed across an entire row, we are going to assign a thread block for each row.

It has been revealed that when compared to out-of-the-box pytorch, the bare bones version of this kernel brings about a 10x speedup. But this is not enough: there are still many optimizations we can add on top of this.

Sources indicate that in terms of latency, one of the most costly operation is accessing VRAM, also called global memory. Luckily, there are some easy-to-follow principles that can dramatically reduce the cost of loading data.

Industry observers note that first, we can take a look at how much data a single thread can load in a single instruction: using the MI300X instruction guide, we see that the largest load we can make from global memory is 128 bits wide. Since we are loading FP16 data, we are going to load 128b / 16b = 8 elements per load. For fp32 elements, it would correspond to 4 elements per load.

Sources indicate that secondly, we make sure memory accesses are coalesced. Since each thread is part of a warp, when one thread reaches a “load” instruction, all other threads in the warp do too. For efficiency’s sake, these “load” instructions are then bundled together across the warp. The warp then collectively fetches the data needed and each thread gets the data it requires. Maximum efficiency is reached when the warp fetches a single chunk of data without any gap in it: this is what we call contiguous data. An issue arises when we need to load more data that can be loaded in one “load” instruction, and is illustrated below.

Recent findings suggest that in this hypothetical scenario, we have two threads in the same warp. They need to collectively load 16 fp32 elements, without constraint on which thread loads which element. This is a typical “reduction” situation. Since a thread can only load 4 fp32 elements per instruction, we have at least two ways of reading the data, represented in scenario (a) and (b). To decide which scenario is best, we need to look at this from warp perspective, not thread perspective. In scenario (a), the first load fetches elements 0,1,2,3,8,9,10,11 : we see that the data is not contiguous, because there is a gap between elements 3 and 8. While in scenario (b), the first load fetches elements 0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7 : we load contiguous data. Same goes for the second load. Thus scenario (b) is better. Although in scenario (a) we end up with 8 contiguous elements per thread, this does not matter: what matters is whether or not the warp loads contiguous data. This matters because if the warp can only load 8 contiguous elements in one cycle, then each load of scenario (a) is processed in two cycles, while in scenario (b), each load only needs the one cycle.

Third, we reduce the number of stores: when we look at steps (1) and (3) we can see that there are only two stores needed: one for r r r and one for xQ x_Q xQ​ . After step (1) we can already store r r r and be done with that. But we still need to access the modified version of x x x after step (2) is done. To do that, we can store the modified version of x x x in global memory and reload it after step (2) is done and rely on cache hits when reloading it. Or, if x x x is small enough, we can store its modified version in shared memory: if x x x is in FP16 and we only have one thread block per CU, then we can store 64KB / 2B = 32 * 1024 elements in shared memory per thread block. In the case of Llama 405B, d d d is equal to 16384, so that fits. Using shared memory provides a nice speedup over relying on cache hits, especially when many thread blocks are active at once: if the L1 cache is not massive enough to fit the whole of x x x, then we have to rely on L2 cache, which is shared by 38 CUs.

Apart from memory access, we can also optimize computational efficiency, but we are going to leave that for the next kernel, as they will be similar in both cases.

When we apply the optimizations discussed above, we get the following results:.

with a [X, 16384] shaped FP16 input tensor. The most basic version of our kernel, referred to as “Pointwise”, has no memory-related optimization and already indicates at least a x4 speedup over torch. It is less optimal than VLLM’s implementation of the kernel, but our “Vectorized” implementation beats both “Pointwise” and VLLM. This is the version of the kernel that implements coalesced 128 bits loads, which is only surpassed by the “Vectorized + SMEM” (SMEM stands for shared memory) implementation, that offers a notably better speedup ratio than VLLM for both low and high batch sizes.

It has been revealed that in the MLP block, after the kernel we have just written about, comes a projection which we have referred up to this point as “Gate / Up” projection. The reason we call it that way is because the “Gate / Up” projection is actually a concatenation of two projections with the same input: “Gate” and “Up”. Thus, we will write the result x x x of the “Gate / Up” projection as x=xG∣xU x = x_G | x_U x=xG​∣xU​ where ∣ | ∣ is the concatenation operator applied along the column axis. xG x_G xG​ and xU x_U xU​ have the same dimensions. The reason we need those two projections is the SwiGLU activation function that comes right after, which results y y y is defined by equation (4). The SwiGLU activation function is followed by the “Down” projection, which in our case is in FP8, so we also need to quantize y y y as shown in equation (5):.

i+j+ky=σ(xG)⋅xUyQ=QFP8(s∗y) \begin{align} \phantom{i + j + k}& \begin{aligned} y = \sigma \left( x_G \right) \cdot x_U \\\end{aligned}\\ &\begin{aligned} y_Q = Q_\text{FP8} \left( s * y \right) \end{aligned} \end{align} i+j+k​y=σ(xG​)⋅xU​​yQ​=QFP8​(s∗y)​​​.

According to recent reports, where σ \sigma σ is the sigmoid function: σ(x)=e−x/(1+x) \sigma (x) = e^{-x} / (1 + x) σ(x)=e−x/(1+x) . We are going to write a fused kernel that takes care of all of this. For this kernel, optimizations described for the RMS kernel are still relevant with the expection of the shared memory buffer. We will focus here on computation-related optimizations.

There are two ways we are going to increase the speed of our kernels: increase the volume of work done for each instruction executed and use faster instructions.

In a recent development, to increase the amount of work done per instruction, we can use packed instructions. Packed instruction are useful when we want to apply the same operator on several elements: rather than executing one instruction per element, we execute one instruction over a vector of element. In a CPU, packed (or vectorized) instructions are the bread-and-butter of single-threaded optimization, as the AVX family of instruction can attest to. There are a few packed instructions on GPU, but they can be quite useful in the right place. On the MI300X there is, among others, packed instruction for FP16 addition and multiplication, which we will use for both steps. There also exists packed conversion from FP32 to FP8, which can provide a nice boost in performance when compared to non-packed conversion. As a matter of fact, there is no conversion from any other data type than FP32 to FP8, so for the RMS norm kernel and this one, we have to go to FP32 precision in order to convert to FP8.

However this is not an problem in this kernel: the sigmoid function σ \sigma σ require us to compute an exponent, which is an operation that greatly benefits from FP32 precision. And this is in an instance where we can optimize computation by using a faster instruction: instead of using the exp instruction, we scale the input by log(2) \text{log}(2) log(2) and use the exp2 instruction, which is much faster. We suffer an almost negligible loss in precision but also reduce latency.

We get the following table for a [X, 16384] shaped FP16 input tensor:.

With memory and compute optimizations tailored for the MI300X, we get a kernel that is more than 14 times faster than Torch on average and from 27% to 100% faster than VLLM’s kernel.

Sources indicate that as we have seen earlier, about 60% of the model’s inference latency comes from projections, which rely on GEMM kernels. GEMM kernels are heavily optimized in dedicated libraries such as hipBLASLT rocBLAS on AMD, so writing a custom kernel that performs better in all cases is quite hard. But if we focus on some edge cases that are relevant to us, and write a GEMM kernel for those specific cases, then there is a chance our custom kernel may be faster than the ones in the dedicated libraries.

In both prefill and decoding, the input of any of the network’s projection has as many rows as there tokens being processed. And during decoding, the number of tokens being processed is equal to the batch size. So during decoding, the number of input rows of all GEMM kernels is equal to the batch size, which for our purposes ranges between 1 and 256. We are going to take an interest with very low batch sizes. When we have a GEMM A∗B=C A * B = C A∗B=C such that A A A has few rows and many columns, we say that the GEMM is skinny. The reason we have a specific term for such GEMMs is that they are ill-fitted for the classic GEMM algorithm we run on GPU. Usually, the efficiency of GEMM kernels comes from tiling: we divide the result matrix in many sub-matrices, called tiles, and we assign each tile to a different compute unit (CU). If we have many tiles, we can use many CUs and GPU usage is high. This is illustrated in the figure below.

But if the input A A A has very few rows, then only a few tiles can be formed, which results in only a few compute units active, hence low GPU utilization:.

Skinny GEMMs are fundamentally inconvenient for the GPU. In the next part, we are going to see how through a custom kernel that assumes we are in a skinny GEMM context, we can make them more convenient.

Recent findings suggest that since the main issue of skinny GEMMs is that we use too few compute units, the first thing we can do is figure out a way to use more. To do this, we can exploit the following mind-breaking formula:.

cij=∑k=1Kaikbkj=(∑k=1K/2aikbkj)+(∑k=1+K/2Kaikbkj) c_{ij} = \sum_{k=1}^K a_{ik} b_{kj} = \left( \sum_{k=1}^{K/2} a_{ik} b_{kj} \right) + \left( \sum_{k=1+K/2}^{K} a_{ik} b_{kj} \right) cij​=k=1∑K​aik​bkj​=​k=1∑K/2​aik​bkj​​+​k=1+K/2∑K​aik​bkj​​.

Industry observers note that thanks to the associativity of the sum, we can split the main GEMM along the shared axis (commonly referred to as the K axis) and replace one GEMM with several sub-GEMMs that are executed concurrently. Each sub-GEMM is going to use as many CUs as the main one would have, so the number of CUs used is multiplied by the number of times we split the K axis. This is shown in the figure below:.

Here, we set split K equal to 2 and thus double the amount of CU used at once. Since we get partial results, we need to add them up after the both sub-GEMMs are done. What may seem counter-intuitive is that we are adding an operation, summing the partial results, yet we claim to reduce the latency of the overall process. But since each CU needs to go through the entire K axis to compute the result, because we are cutting it in two, the amount of work done by each CU is also cut in two. If the amount of work saved this way counter balances the amount of work added by the summing up of the final results, then we have an overall optimization. This is generally true as long as K is large and the original GEMM uses less than 50% of the GPU.

It has been revealed that if we assume that through split-K, most compute units are busy with their own tile, we can focus the scope of optimization at the compute unit level. We are going to take a look at how the actual matrix multiplication is done, and how we can accelerate it.

In a recent development, in state of the art GPUs like the MI300X, matrix multiplication is handled by a dedicated hardware unit called tensor cores. Tensor cores only perform matrix multiplications, but they do so at very high speed. The format of tensor core instruction is mfma_MxNxK... where mfma stands for matrix fused multiply-add, M is the number of rows of the left-hand matrix, N the number of column of the right-hand matrix, and K is the shared dimension of both. We illustrate a hypothetical instruction mfma_2x2x4 below:.

There are only a few tensor core instructions, but for any triplet MxNxK using the dedicated tensor core instruction is much faster than any other alternative. Tensor core instruction also come in two flavours: “dense” and “sparse”. Dense instruction correspond to standard matrix multiplication. Sparse instructions assume that the left-hand side matrix A A A has a 4:2 structured sparsity pattern, which means that two out of every 4 elements along the matrix K axis are zero. Mathematically, for any i,j i, j i,j such that ai,4j+3 a_{i, 4j+3} ai,4j+3​ is an element of A A A , we have at least two zeros in (ai,4j,ai,4j+1,ai,4j+2,ai,4j+3) \left( a_{i,4j}, a_{i,4j+1}, a_{i,4j+2}, a_{i,4j+3} \right) (ai,4j​,ai,4j+1​,ai,4j+2​,ai,4j+3​) . Below is an example of a sparse matrix.

Recent findings suggest that let’s get back to our model, Llama 405B in FP8. For FP8, we only have two dense tensor core instruction: 16x16x32 and 32x32x16 . We also have one sparse instruction of size 16x16x64 . For an input with 8 rows, using even the smallest dense instruction 16x16x32 means that we have to add 8 rows of padding to our input, which is a waste of compute resources. One can wonder if we can use the sparse instruction instead: after all, if half of a 16 rows matrix is 4:2 sparse, we can fully describe its non-zero coefficients using a dense 8 rows matrix. Conversely, if we have an 8 rows dense matrix, we can fit all of its data into a 16 rows matrix with 4:2 sparsity. And the benefit of using the sparse instruction is obvious: the dense instruction has K=32 while the sparse instruction has K=64 . For the same amount of cycles, the sparse instruction has twice the depth. We illustrate this sparsity trick in the figure below with a 1 row input and the 2x2x4 dense instruction and its sparse 2x2x8 counterpart.

Using this trick, we can notably speed up our GEMM for any input with 8 or less rows, which results in a reduction in per-token latency for any decoding batch that has less than 8 requests.

Sources indicate that we have seen that in a skinny GEMM, the fact we have a little number of rows limits the number of output tiles, which in turns limit the GPU utilization. But the small number of rows also limits the number of rows each output tiles has, which in turns reduces what we call arithmetic intensity. Simply put, arithmetic intensity is the amount of work done divided by the amount of data loaded to do that work. Let us compare two examples:.

sn=∑i=1nxitn=∑i=1nyi=y (1+tn−1) s_n = \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i \\ t_n = \sum_{i=1}^n y^i = y ~( 1 + t_{n-1}) sn​=i=1∑n​xi​tn​=i=1∑n​yi=y (1+tn−1​).

where x x x is an n n n -sized vector and y y y is a scalar. To compute sn s_n sn​ , we load n n n elements and perform n−1 n-1 n−1 additions. To compute tn t_n tn​ , we load 1 element and perform 2n−1 2n-1 2n−1 additions and multiplications. So the “arithmetic intensity” of computing sn s_n sn​ is n−1n \frac{n-1}{n} nn−1​ while tn t_n tn​ is 2n−1 2n - 1 2n−1 : the computation of tn t_n tn​ is more “arithmetically intensive” than the computation of sn s_n sn​ . What we see here is that when the lower arithmetic intensity is, the more data we need to load to perform work.

Sources indicate that why does this matter to us? Well, we have seen that loading data from VRAM has a high latency cost, which is not great for the GPU. In other words, workloads with low arithmetic intensity are ill-suited for the GPU, and it turns out skinny GEMMs have lower arithmetic intensity than their non-skinny counterparts. This becomes intuitive when looking at the figure below: we can see that when we divide the amount of data loaded by two, we divide the number of output coefficients by 4, due to the quadratic nature of the GEMM’s dimensions.

Sources indicate that in a skinny GEMM the number of rows of the output tile is limited and so is the arithmetic intensity. Already this means that we are going to need to load a lot of data to compute an output tile. Furthermore, since we are using FP8 arithmetic, computation is quite fast, so we cannot rely on computation time to hide the latency of data loading. All in all, it would be ideal to have more threads in charge of loading data than threads in charge of computing the result.

In a recent development, to achieve this, we are going to use a technique called warp specialization. Instead having all warps in the thread block execute the same instructions, we are going to dedicate some warps to loading data only and some to computing the results only. The warps in charge of loading data are called producers and the ones that compute the results are named consumers. Producers and consumers work asynchronously: producers first load data from the VRAM, which is slow, and make it available to the consumers by storing it in a shared memory buffer. Until data is available in shared memory, the consumer is idle. After it data is made available, the consumer loads it from shared memory, which is fast, and computes the result. Coordination of producers and consumers is achieved through a queue stored in shared memory. When a producer finishes storing data in a shared memory buffer i i i , it changes the state of the i i i th variable of the queue to signal data is available there. The consumer is watching out for this, and begins loading data afterwards. When it is done, it changes the i i i th variable of the queue to signal that data can be written over in buffer i i i . In the figure below, we represent the steps involved in a simple asynchronous GEMM with one producer, one consumer and a queue of size 2.

What makes the whole process work is that once buffer 0 0 0 is filled by a producer, it can start working on buffer 1 1 1 without waiting for the consumer to have loaded the data from buffer 0 0 0. The goal is to have a queue large enough for the producers to be constantly filling buffers and consumers constantly consuming them. The size of queue is constrained by the size of the shared memory.

According to recent reports, we also need to tune the ratio of producers to consumers: we have mentioned that we have a low arithmetic intensity, so we need to load a lot of data to do a relatively fast computation. Hence, we are going to have a lot of producer warps (typically 8 or 10) for a few consumer warps (something like 2 or 3). Furthermore, we can exploit the fact the GEMM is skinny by having separate producers for the input (the skinny matrix) and the weights (the non-skinny matrix). To make the output tile bigger in the dimension in which it is not constrained in, which is the columns dimension, we allocate more producers for the weights.

For a more in-depth blog post about asynchronous GEMMs, I encourage you to check out this blog post. A lot of its contents are not applicable in our case though: the MI300X has no warp-level barriers, only a single thread block-level barrier. This led to “fun” shenanigans like ASM to ensure warps waited at their barriers, shared memory loads and stores were resolved before checking the barrier state, and careful handling of the modular nature of the queue. All this would be out of place here, but I encourage you to check out the code or ask away in the comments. A deep dive on the details of async handling might be coming in the future.

According to recent reports, through warp specialization and asynchronous work, we can adapt our kernel to the low arithmetic intensity workload, but is that enough to come ahead of libraries like hipBLASLT? The answer is yes, in some cases.

Sources indicate that since Torch already binds a highly optimized GEMM taken from AMD’s linear algebra library, we are not going to get speedups in the same range as for the two last kernels. We are first going to take a look at the three GEMM dimension that are of interest to us: namely, the GEMMs dimensions associated with the QKV projection, the Gate / Up projection and the Down projection. The Output projection is being left out because its dimensions do not correspond to the skinny GEMM case.

Measures are taken after 500 warmups iterations, over 2000 profiling iterations, using CUDA graph and multiple weights to avoid cache hits. In order, the GEMM dimensions shown above correspond to QKV projection (N = 2304 and K = 16384), Gate / Up projection (N = 13312 and K = 16384) and Down projection (N= 16384 and K = 6656). We can see that for those dimensions, which have been tuned for, there is a notable speedup for low number of rows (M = 1, 8, 16) but less so for more rows (M = 32). Especially for dimensions in which we can use our sparsity trick (M = 1, 8) we see a notable speedup over Torch, which probably pads everything to 16 rows to use the smallest MFMA instruction.

In this post, we explored just a handful of the many kernel optimization techniques available. If you're interested in experimenting with them, feel free to dive into the hf-rocm-kernels repository and start tinkering! And if you develop a kernel you like of and want to distribute it, be sure to check out kernel-builder and kernels — two Hugging Face packages designed to help kernel builders make their work widely available and more impactful.

Great work! For the Skinny GEMM, do you have numbers for % improvements from sparse mfma and warp specialization (WS) separately? Trying to understand what the impact of WS for different shapes, without sparse mfma.

Recent findings suggest that looking at the code, my understanding is that sparsity is only used for M = 8. Is this correct?

How does the async handling work?

Sources indicate that we use an int16 variable in the shared memory (a semaphore), which can be looked up by any warp on the SM. The thing you have to be carefull about is to have all instructions related to SMEM or GMEM finished before changing the state of the semaphore. For instance, you have to explicitly wait for SMEM stores to be over before switching the semaphore.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Knoxville Police Department has announced its “Drone as First Responder” program, or DFR, with semi-autonomous drones set to be debuted from 12 docks located around the city. The docks will allow drones to be dispatched within seconds of a 911 call being received, and they will be able to reach nearly any area of the city within just 90 seconds, according to a page on the police department's website. It's hoped that the drones will be able to reduce the risk to the community as well as police officers, while providing real-time situational awareness during "rapidly evolving events.".

Sources indicate that while the police department hasn't confirmed which drones will be used, we do know that they will be debuted from Skydio docks located at city-owned facilities. It's expected that the drones will, in some cases, reach the scene more quickly than the police officer they are supposed to accompany. This should give officers vital information related to the scene that they are about to attend.

While drones won't be dispatched to all 911 calls, the department indicates that they will be sent in response to 911 calls in which aerial coverage may be of use to the overall response. That includes enhancing the safety of the officers attending as well as public safety.The latest drones will no doubt raise concerns about privacy. The department says that they will not be used for surveillance, pointing out that department policy and state law prohibit the drones from being used for random patrols or surveillance. They also don't possess any kind of facial recognition or license plate reader technologies. While the drones will, of course, capture video, the department's FAQ page notes that any recorded footage will be purged after 15 days. That is, unless it is retained as evidence for use in an ongoing criminal investigation or prosecution.

Knoxville isn't the first to turn to drones in this way. Several cities were reportedly experimenting with using Flock's own DFR system last month. Companies have also been advertising Starlink-connected first responder drones for some time.

Tech Report: Power BI MCP server: how to brief an AI agent to build accurate measures

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3048 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • Industry observers note that weekly.
  • Power BI, Microsoft's reporting and dashboard tool, now lets an AI agent work on the data model behind a report.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Industry observers note that weekly. Free. One click to leave.

7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

Power BI, Microsoft's reporting and dashboard tool, now lets an AI agent work on the data model behind a report. If you ask one to add a year-on-year revenue measure (a measure is Power BI's name for a saved calculation) with Microsoft's MCP server connected, it can write the formula and save it to the model without you opening the formula bar. When we tried this on a sample model, an agent inspected the model, wrote the measure, tested it and saved it in under four minutes.

In a recent development, the agent did a careful job, but its formula didn't follow the same rules the finance team uses to count revenue. Nobody had told it what "revenue" meant in this business, so it had to decide for itself. We then gave another agent a short brief that set out finance's rules for what counts as revenue and which date to count it by. The agent wrote the formula from those rules, and the result matched finance's figure exactly. The two results show how much difference it makes in how you brief an AI agent to build accurate measures.

Recent findings suggest that we wanted to find out what an agent can see in a Power BI model and how to brief it so the measure matches the business's own definitions, with the setup arranged so that every change can be checked. Developers will know the principle from agents that write SQL or API code, where the brief ends up doing the job of a specification.

Because MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard, the same server can be used from different AI clients, GitHub Copilot in VS Code and Claude among them, although some clients need extra sign-in setup for the hosted version.

According to recent reports, power BI has two current MCP servers, plus an older one, the Power BI Consumption MCP server, kept for existing integrations. The first of the current pair is the Power BI Authoring MCP server, which you may still see under the name of its package, powerbi-modeling-mcp. It lets an agent create and change the objects inside a semantic model, which is the layer of a Power BI report that holds the tables, the relationships between them and the calculations, kept separate from the charts on the page. It comes in two forms. The hosted version, still in preview, needs nothing installed. The local version is generally available and runs on your own machine, which makes it the one to use when the model is a file you hold yourself, whether that's open in Power BI Desktop, the free Windows app used to build reports, or saved as a project folder. Macs aren't supported by the local version, so on a Mac it has to be the hosted one, which works only with models published to Microsoft's cloud (a Fabric workspace).

The second is the Fabric IQ MCP server. Fabric IQ is part of Microsoft Fabric, the wider data platform that Power BI now sits within. It gives an agent read-only tools for finding published reports and models and running queries against them, within the permissions already set, so the agent can answer questions about the data but can't change a model.

Which one to use follows from the job. Anything that changes a model goes through the authoring server, whether that's a newly introduced measure, a relationship or a set of descriptions, and it has to be the local version if the model is a Desktop file or a project folder under source control. Fabric IQ is for agents that only need answers from models other people maintain.

Sources indicate that an agent connected to a semantic model can see its metadata (table and column names, data types, relationships, existing measures and any descriptions someone has written) and can run queries against the data. Everything it produces is inferred from those clues. A model that has served a business for years carries names that made perfect sense to the people who built it, and a column called Amt on a table called Sales_v2 tells an agent far less than it tells them.

Names carry a lot of the meaning. A column called Amount could hold the value with VAT (the UK's sales tax) or without, before credit notes or after, and an agent asked for "revenue" has to pick one. If the model holds several revenue measures built for different reports, the agent has to choose between them, and the one it picks may have been built for a different purpose.

The formulas depend on context as well. Power BI measures use a syntax of their own called DAX, which stands for Data Analysis Expressions. A DAX result shifts with whatever the person viewing the report has filtered or clicked on, which is known as filter context. A developer might think of a measure as a function that reads implicit state set by its caller. The same measure can be right as a single total on a card and need different handling once it's split by product in a table or filtered by a date slicer (the on-page date filter), depending on how CALCULATE (the DAX function that changes which filters apply) is used. Which behaviour is correct depends on how the business wants the number to respond, and that's something the agent has to be told.

Recent findings suggest that relationships work the same way. Plenty of models have more than one date column on the sales table, say order date and dispatch date, with only one relationship active at a time. A DAX measure uses the active relationship unless it's written to switch to the other one, and the agent has no way of knowing which date your monthly reporting runs on unless something tells it.

In a recent development, in each case the agent can write a valid measure. Which of two valid measures matches the business's own definition is the part it can't see from the model.

To see this in practice, we built a small sales model in a Power BI Desktop file, working through the server itself, with invented data: 5,266 order lines, with order dates from January 2025 to October 2026. We gave the Sales table an Amt column holding each line's value after discount with 20% VAT added, next to LineTotal and Discount columns that excluded VAT, and an existing [Revenue] measure that summed Amt. There were two date columns, with the active relationship to the Date table on dispatch date and the order date relationship inactive. Orders stop at the end of October 2026, which made the current year a part year, a deliberate test. Nothing in the model had a description. In this made-up business, finance reports revenue net of VAT and discounts, by order date.

In a recent development, on 12 November 2026 we connected an AI agent (Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2) to version 1.0.1 of the local server through a small Node.js script that speaks MCP over stdio. In all three runs the agent had the server's tools only, without Microsoft's powerbi-authoring plugin, which adds modelling guidance on top of them. It was also told that nobody was available to answer questions, so each measure was saved exactly as the agent wrote it, with no review in between. The first prompt was one sentence: "Add a year-on-year revenue measure.".

According to recent reports, before writing anything, the agent listed the tables, relationships and columns, read the existing measure, sampled some rows and checked the date ranges. It worked out for itself that 2026 was a part year and limited the comparison to the same dates in 2025, which avoided a misleading result of -6.7%. From 15 sample rows it also spotted that Amt looked like the net figure plus 20%.

It has been revealed that the measure it saved reused the existing [Revenue] measure and followed the active relationship. This is the core of it, with the date handling and blank checks left out. CurrentDates is defined in those lines as the dates up to the last order:.

It returned growth of 21.5% for 2026, which is correct for revenue counted by dispatch date. On finance's definition, by order date, the answer is 18.6%, and the whole difference came from that choice of date. The VAT question made no difference to a percentage, because Amt was already net of discount and every line carried the same rate, although it would have overstated any figure in pounds by 20%.

Recent findings suggest that we reset the model and repeated the run with a fresh agent, which made the same two choices and returned the same 21.5%. Both choices were reasonable readings of the model as it stood, and the DAX was sound. In their reports, both agents flagged the date basis and the VAT treatment as open questions, and both worked out that an order-date basis would give 18.6%. That's what a good analyst would do, and with those two answers they would have had everything they needed.

Think of a capable analyst on their first morning, someone who knows DAX well but has never seen your business before and knows nothing (or not a lot) about it. You wouldn't say "add a revenue measure" and walk off. You'd tell them which table holds the trusted figures, whether revenue includes VAT, which date drives the reporting calendar, and what they shouldn't touch. An agent needs that briefing for the same reasons, and getting good work out of it draws on the skills you'd use with any new starter. Developers do the same thing when they write a good ticket. A request for a measure is a requirement, and it needs the same definitions and constraints, plus a way to check the result.

Before you send a prompt, ask yourself whether you could do the task properly if you were given only the words in that prompt and the model itself. If the answer is no, then the agent is in the same position, and it will make its own assumptions.

For the detailed run we cleared the earlier measure from the model and gave a fresh agent this brief:.

In a recent development, this time the measure summed LineTotal minus Discount and used USERELATIONSHIP, the DAX function that switches a calculation to an inactive relationship, to work from order date. It returned 18.6% from that one brief, with no follow-up prompt, which is the figure we had calculated separately from the source data. This is the full measure as the agent saved it:.

Each line of the brief answered a question the agent would otherwise have had to settle alone. It also made some sensible decisions the brief hadn't covered. It left the grand total blank, for instance, where a plain total across both years would have shown a meaningless growth figure of 151.2%. The final line of the brief, asking to see the DAX before anything is saved, is there so that a person can see choices like that. In the test we approved that step in advance, to keep the run unattended.

Recent findings suggest that one detail needs adjusting before this measure is reused on other data. Its guard checks that each comparison period starts on or after the first order date, which works here because the sample data has an order on 1 January 2025. When we swapped that date for 2 January 2025 in a copy of the measure, January 2026 and the 2026 row came back blank. Comparing against the first date in the Date table, as the first agent's measure did, brought the 2026 figure back, since the Date table starts on 1 January. That version doesn't confirm that sales exist for the whole comparison period, though, so the right check depends on whether the business wants growth shown only where a complete prior period exists. That's a decision for whoever reviews the measure.

We ran the one-sentence prompt twice and the detailed brief once, all with the same AI model and one small set of data, which is enough to illustrate the pattern but too little to say how often it happens.

In a recent development, good briefs help, but you'll be writing the same definitions into prompts again and again unless they live in the model itself. Descriptions on tables, columns and measures are part of the metadata the agent reads, so filling them in is one of the cheapest ways to put business definitions in front of it every time. In our test, where nothing had a description, both agents given the one-sentence prompt noted that nothing confirmed what Amt contained. A description such as "Net sales value in GBP, excluding VAT, after credit notes" stays in the model, where the agent reads it without anyone retyping it.

Naming deserves the same attention. Spelling out abbreviated column names, hiding technical keys that no report needs, gathering measures into a single measures table, and removing measures that are no longer used all give the agent fewer things to choose between. These are the same habits that make a model easier for a fresh colleague to pick up, so asking someone outside the team to find a figure in it is a fair test of the result.

Microsoft has also added a set of Prep data for AI features (in preview) to Power BI Desktop and the service. They let you choose which fields Copilot, Microsoft's AI assistant, should consider and write AI instructions that explain your business terms, with verified answers available for common questions. They're aimed at Copilot, but deciding and writing down your definitions is the same work whichever AI tool reads them.

Sources indicate that an agent working through the authoring server has the same access as the person signed in, so anything that person can change, the agent can change. Sign in with an account that has no more access than the job needs, and take a copy of the model first, as you would before any bulk edit.

Industry observers note that start with read-only mode. The local server takes a --readonly flag that blocks all write operations, which is the right setting while you're learning how the agent behaves on your models. When we tried to create a measure in this mode, the server refused and remarked it was running read-only. In VS Code, the configuration looks like this (other clients use a similar structure, sometimes under an mcpServers key instead of servers):.

You'll need Node.js installed for the npx command. The server won't run other tools until its licence terms (the EULA) have been accepted. Once you've read them, you can either tell the agent to accept for you or add --accepteula to the args list.

The --readonly flag belongs to the local server. On a Mac the route is the hosted server and a copy of the model in a Fabric workspace, once a Fabric administrator has switched on the tenant setting that allows the MCP endpoint, and there the copy is the safeguard. For an enforced limit, sign in with an account that holds only Build permission on the model, which lets the agent read and query it and nothing more.

It has been revealed that read-write is the default, so check how confirmation behaves in the version you install. Version 1.0.1 skips confirmation prompts by default, which the project's README hasn't caught up with, and has a --require-confirmation flag to turn them on. The flag is listed in the server's own --help output. In our runs every edit went through without a prompt. When we added the flag to the args list, the server asked for confirmation before the first write, with a message beginning "Are you sure you want to perform operations that will modify your database", and answering no blocked the change.

Version control is the other safeguard. Saved in the Power BI Project format (PBIP), a report and its model become folders of text files instead of one binary .pbix file. Commit those before the agent starts and its work arrives as an ordinary diff, which you can review and revert like any other change.

Whatever the agent reads, including table and column names and the rows returned by any query, is passed on to the AI provider behind your client, which may sit outside Microsoft's compliance commitments. For a model holding customer or payroll data, check that the provider is approved under your data policies before you connect.

An agent can draft and test a measure in minutes, and someone still has to read what comes back. For a developer upcoming to Power BI, that takes enough DAX to see what a measure's filters will do in a table broken down by month or product, and enough knowledge of the business to confirm the agent used the right column and the right date. Writing the brief takes the same knowledge. Ours could only have come from someone who knew the model had an inactive relationship and which columns carried VAT.

Sources indicate that these are data modelling and DAX skills, which many learners find the hardest part of Power BI. If the person reviewing agent output hasn't had that grounding yet, it helps to know how to judge whether a Power BI course covers enough DAX and data modelling, because courses vary a great deal in how much time they give to those two subjects compared with building charts.

Take a copy of a model you know well and connect the local server to it in read-only mode. Ask the agent to describe every table and measure in its own words, then check those descriptions against what you know the model does. Wherever the two differ, the model needs a clearer name or a written description, and the corrected text can go straight into the description fields. With those in place before you allow any writes, the agent starts its first real task with the same definitions your finance team uses.

Show, Don't Certify: How to Prepare for Your First Data Analyst Job

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1564 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • According to recent reports, weekly.
  • Getting shortlisted for a junior data analyst job depends less on how many courses you have finished and more on what you can show.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

According to recent reports, weekly. Free. One click to leave.

7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

Getting shortlisted for a junior data analyst job depends less on how many courses you have finished and more on what you can show. This initiative breaks preparation into eight skill areas, pairs each one with a learning option and a hands-on task, and gives you a simple test for knowing when to move on.

Many people preparing for their first analyst role study for months and still struggle to get interviews. Their CVs list SQL, Excel and Tableau, yet nothing on the page indicates those tools being used to answer a real question. Recruiters reading dozens of similar applications need something more concrete.

A course can give your learning a sensible order, but a completion badge claims little about how you think. A small analysis that states its question, explains its method and admits its limits tells a hiring manager far more. This proposal aims to collect that kind of proof while you learn, not after.

Start by collecting ten to twenty entry-level postings in the industry you want to join, and tally the tools and tasks they mention. You will promptly see a pattern. Some roles are built around Excel and routine reporting, while others want SQL, a BI platform and a bit of Python.

Sources indicate that the wider market follows a similar shape. Jobright’s 2026 analysis of data analyst hiring, which looked at 2025–2026 postings from LinkedIn, Indeed and Levels.fyi, found that more than 80% of data analyst jobs mention SQL, over 60% mention Excel or Google Sheets, and roughly half mention Python or R. Let your own tally decide the order you learn in, but expect SQL to sit near the top.

As you work through each area below, finish with something you can show someone: a query, a tidied dataset, a chart, a one-page report or a portfolio project. Free material is often enough if you can stay disciplined. Pay for teaching only when it gives you something you cannot get alone, such as feedback, accountability or a fixed timetable.

Recent findings suggest that SQL is how analysts pull, join and summarise records from a database, and a tool like Tableau lets other people explore what you found. Treat them as one workflow rather than two subjects: frame a question, write the query, sanity-check the numbers and present the result so a non-technical reader can follow it.

SQLBolt offers free, bite-sized SQL lessons that run in the browser, and Tableau publishes free training videos on connecting to data and building dashboards. Used together, they are enough to produce a small end-to-end project.

In a recent development, if you learn better with a set schedule and an instructor checking your work, you could learn to analyse data with SQL and Tableau from scratch through a guided programme at Heicoders Academy in Singapore. Whichever route you take, compare what is covered, how feedback is given, when sessions run and the full cost against what free resources already offer.

Proof you can show: A working SQL query set and your first published dashboard.

Move on when: You can take a question from idea to dashboard on your own, without following a tutorial line by line.

In a recent development, spreadsheets are still where much of a team’s day-to-day reporting lives, especially when colleagues don’t write SQL. Get comfortable with filtering, pivot tables, and lookup functions, and learn to spot quiet errors like dates saved as text or one category spelled three different ways.

Industry observers note that the next step is automating the cleanup so it doesn’t have to be repeated by hand each month. Microsoft’s Power Query documentation shows how to import and reshape data in recorded steps that refresh when newly introduced data arrives. The same ideas apply in other spreadsheet tools too.

Proof you can show: A messy export turned into a summary that refreshes itself.

Move on when: You can clean an untidy CSV and build a report that updates when the source file changes.

Sources indicate that for most junior analyst roles, the technical interview is a SQL test. Basic SELECT statements won’t be enough; interviewers like to probe joins, subqueries, common table expressions and window functions, which answer everyday questions such as running totals or each customer’s first purchase.

Practise with timed problem sets and review your answers for correctness as well as speed.

Proof you can show: Confidence going into a live or take-home SQL test.

Move on when: You can solve intermediate problems in around 15 to 20 minutes each without looking up syntax.

Take-home assignments often come with data that has been made messy on purpose. Reviewers want to see how you deal with missing values, duplicates and inconsistent formats, and whether they can follow your reasoning afterwards.

In a recent development, keep a short cleaning log as you work, noting each change and why you made it. A separate sheet tab or a list of comments in a notebook both work.

Proof you can show: A take-home submission a reviewer can audit step by step.

Move on when: Every change to your dataset is written down with a reason.

Case-study questions test whether you can read numbers sensibly, not just produce them. A working grasp of distributions, means and medians, spread, correlation and sampling will keep you away from the mistakes that undo otherwise good answers, such as quoting an average that a few extreme values have pulled out of shape.

Proof you can show: Clear, careful answers in case-study interviews.

Move on when: You can explain in everyday language why two things moving together doesn’t mean one causes the other.

In a recent development, every chart should help someone answer a specific question. Learn where bars, lines, scatter plots and simple tables each work best, and how axis ranges, labels and colour can nudge a reader towards the wrong conclusion. On a dashboard, the most important finding should be the first thing people see.

In a recent development, datawrapper’s guidance on picking chart types is a useful free reference. As practice, show the same result in two different chart types and decide which one represents the data more honestly.

Proof you can show: Portfolio charts that make a point, not just show off features.

Move on when: A person who has never seen your data can spot the main finding and its caveat at a glance.

What counts as a useful metric depends on the role. Marketing analysts focus on conversion and retention, operations analysts on delivery times and capacity, and finance analysts on margins and cash flow. Choose one sector and learn exactly how its key measures are defined.

Proof you can show: A project built around the questions your target industry actually asks.

Move on when: You can define several sector metrics and describe how a manager would use each one.

Your portfolio is where the other seven areas come together. Two or three deep, well-documented projects will say more about you than a long list of quick ones. Give each project a README that sets out the question, the data, your method, the findings and the limitations.

Proof you can show: A portfolio link and a write-up you can talk through in an interview.

Move on when: Every project clearly explains what it asked, how you answered it and what you found.

According to recent reports, there is no need to finish all eight areas before you apply. Once you can use the tools your target roles mention, speak honestly about your work and point to two or three clearly explained projects, start sending applications and keep learning alongside them.

Industry observers note that adjust each application to the job. Lead with a reporting example for spreadsheet-heavy roles, a query that solved a real problem for SQL roles, and a chart that supported a decision for visualisation roles. Be upfront about which work you built independently and which came from guided exercises.

According to recent reports, do I really need eight courses? No. These are skill areas, not eight required qualifications. A single resource can cover several of them, and practice you do on your own counts as much as classroom learning.

In a recent development, is it possible to prepare using only free material? Yes. Free tutorials, open textbooks, official documentation and public datasets cover the fundamentals well. The harder parts are sticking to a routine and finding people who will give you honest feedback.

Which should come first, SQL or spreadsheets? It depends on the jobs you want. Spreadsheets are an easy starting point for reporting roles, while SQL is expected wherever databases are involved. You will want both eventually, so start with whichever your target postings stress most.

How many portfolio projects should I have? Two or three solid ones are a good start. Each should show a clear question, steps someone else could repeat and an honest reading of the results, rather than several near-identical dashboards.

Recent findings suggest that do I need a certificate before I apply? Not usually. Some employers ask for one, but many judge skills through interviews, take-home tasks and tests instead. Go by what each posting actually requires.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google introduced 3D emoji on Pixel this year, and has just detailed the minimum specifications required to get them on your Android phone.

Sources indicate that update: Google replied on Reddit to “clear up some confusion” about the Help Center page. The listed storage and RAM requirements refer to the “automatic background download via Google Play services on eligible Android 17 devices that didn’t ship with the 3D font preinstalled.” The support article did not make that distinction.

Noto 3D emoji, with its high-resolution bitmap approach, uses less than 220 MB of storage versus the previous 2D vector font that comes in at around 3 MB.

During installation, Google Play services temporarily needs a bit of extra headroom to copy the file into place before immediately clearing its download cache.

Meanwhile, Google stated RAM usage is “minimal & transient” as “Android doesn’t load the 3D emoji font file into RAM.” The support page listed 6 GB as a “cutoff to ensure lower-memory devices stay on the lightweight ~3 MB 2D vector font.”.

Noto 3D emoji goes from vector-based 2D emoji to a high-resolution bitmap font. This results in “high-resolution designs” for emoji “with more texture and dimension to characters and icons.” Google has an FAQ section about why the upcoming emoji might look low resolution:.

Vector vs. bitmap rendering: Older Android emoji used 2D vector graphics, which scale infinitely to any size without losing resolution. The 3D emoji are bitmap graphics, which are pre-rendered pixel-based images. When these images are scaled up by an app or zoomed in, the pixels stretch, which can cause a softer or lower-resolution appearance.

The Google support article published this week lists the minimum specs your Android device must have to get 3D emoji:.

The last two bullet points are rather surprising. In fact, Google even lists instructions for checking how much memory and storage your device has:.

In terms of availability, Google says a supported device will “automatically download the 3D emoji when it’s on Wi-Fi and charging.”.

At this time, there isn’t a way to force download the emoji.

Sources indicate that google announced 3D emoji in May, with the new design shipping on the Pixel 11 in August. It has since arrived on older Pixel devices.

In terms of OEM availability, Google explicitly states “Samsung devices use a proprietary emoji font and do not receive the 3D font update.” Additionally:.

This is also true for third-party messaging apps, such as WhatsApp, who use their own emoji fonts rather than relying on your device’s system font.

Latest Update: Building the Hugging Face MCP Server

📅 10 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1414 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • TL;DR: The Hugging Face Official MCP Server offers unique customization options for AI Assistants accessing the Hub, along with access to thousands of AI applications through one simple URL.
  • We've learned many things about building a useful MCP server in the last month - we'll describe our journey here.
  • The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is fulfilling its promise of being the standard to connect AI Assistants to the outside world.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TL;DR: The Hugging Face Official MCP Server offers unique customization options for AI Assistants accessing the Hub, along with access to thousands of AI applications through one simple URL. We used MCPs "Streamable HTTP" transport for deployment, and examine in detail the trade-offs that Server Developers have.

We've learned many things about building a useful MCP server in the last month - we'll describe our journey here.

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is fulfilling its promise of being the standard to connect AI Assistants to the outside world.

At Hugging Face, providing access to the Hub via MCP is an obvious choice, and this article shares our experience developing the hf.co/mcp MCP Server.

The community uses the Hub for research, development, content creation and more. We wanted to let people customize the server for their own needs, as well as easily access thousands of AI applications available on Spaces. This meant making the MCP Server dynamic by adjusting consumers' tools on the fly.

We also wanted to make access simple by avoiding complicated downloads and configuration, so making it remotely accessible via a simple URL was a must.

When building a remote MCP Server, the first decision is deciding how clients will connect to it. MCP offers several transport options, with different trade-offs. TL;DR: our open source code supports all variants, but for production we chose to go with the most modern one. This section goes through the different options in detail.

Industry observers note that since its launch in November 2024, MCP has undergone rapid evolution with 3 protocol revisions in 9 months. This has seen the replacement of the SSE Transport with Streamable HTTP, as well as the introduction and rework of authorization.

These rapid changes mean support for different MCP Features and revisions in Client applications varies, providing extra challenges for our design choices.

Here is a brief summary of the Transport Options offered by the Model Context Protocol and associated SDKs:.

Both STDIO and HTTP with SSE are fully bi-directional by default - meaning that Client and Server maintain an open connection and can send messages to each other at any time.

SSE refers to "Server Sent Events" - a way for HTTP Servers to maintain an open connection and send events in response to a request.

MCP Server Developers face a lot of choices when setting up the Streamable HTTP transport.

There are 3 main communication patterns to choose from:.

When using Request Scoped Streams with the official SDKs, use the sendNotification() and sendRequest() methods provided in the RequestHandlerExtra parameter (TypeScript) or set the related_request_id (Python) to send messages to the correct stream.

An additional factor to consider is whether or not the MCP Server itself needs to maintain state for each connection. This is decided by the Server when the Client sends its Initialize request:.

The table below summarizes the MCP Features and their supported communication pattern:.

With Request Scoped streams, Sampling and Elicitation requests need a Stateful connection so that the mcp-session-id can be used for response association.

The Hugging Face MCP Server is Open Source - and supports STDIO, SSE and Streamable HTTP deployment in both Direct Response and Server Push mode. You can configure keep-alive and last activity timeouts when using Server Push Streams. There's also a built-in observability dashboard that you can use to understand how different Clients manage connections, and handle Tool List change notifications.

The following picture shows our MCP Server connection dashboard running in "Server Push" Streamable HTTP mode:.

For production, we decided to launch our MCP Server with Streamable HTTP in a Stateless, Direct Response configuration for the following reasons:.

According to recent reports, stateless For anonymous users we supply a standard set of Tools for using the Hub along with an Image Generator. For authenticated users our state comprises their selected tools and chosen Gradio applications. We also make sure that users ZeroGPU quota is correctly applied for their account. This is managed using the supplied HF_TOKEN or OAuth credentials that we look up on request. None of our existing tools require us to maintain any other state between requests.

Recent findings suggest that you can use OAuth login by adding ?login to the MCP Server url - e.g. https://huggingface.co/mcp?login. We may make this the default once the claude.ai remote integration supports the latest OAuth spec.

Direct Response provides the lowest deployment resource overhead - and we don't right now have any Tools that require Sampling or Elicitation during execution.

In a recent development, future Support At launch, the "HTTP with SSE" transport was still the remote default in a lot of MCP Clients. However, we didn't want to invest heavily in managing it due to its imminent deprecation. Fortunately, popular clients had already started making the switch (VSCode and Cursor), and within a week of launch claude.ai also added support. If you need to connect with SSE, feel free to deploy a copy of our Server on a FreeCPU Hugging Face Space.

In the future, we would like to support real-time Tool List Changed notifications when consumers revision their settings on the Hub. However, this raises a couple of practical problems:.

Recent findings suggest that first, customers tend to configure their favourite MCP Servers in their Client and leave them enabled. This means that the Client remains connected whilst the application is open. Sending notifications would mean maintaining as many open connections as there were right now active Clients - regardless of active usage - on the chance the user updates their tool configuration.

It has been revealed that second, most MCP Servers and Clients disconnect after a period of inactivity, resuming when necessary. This inevitably means that immediate push notifications would be missed - as the notification channel will have been closed. In practice, it is far simpler for the Client to refresh the connection and Tool List as needed.

Unless you have reasonable control over the Client/Server pair, using Server Push Streams adds a lot of complexity to a public deployment, when lower-resource solutions for refreshing the Tool List exist.

Just before launch, @julien-c submitted a PR to include friendly instructions for customers visiting hf.co/mcp. This hugely improves the User Experience - the default response is otherwise an unfriendly bit of JSON.

According to recent reports, initially, we found this generated an enormous amount of traffic. After a bit of investigation we found that when returning a web page rather than an HTTP 405 error, VSCode would poll the endpoint multiple times per second!

The fix suggested by @coyotte508 was to properly detect browsers and only return the page in that circumstance. Thanks also to the VSCode team who rapidly fixed it.

Although not specifically stated - returning a page in this manner does seem acceptable within the MCP Specification.

The MCP Protocol sends several requests during initialization. A typical connection sequence is: Initialize, Notifications/Initialize, tools/list and then prompts/list.

Given that MCP Clients will connect and reconnect whilst open, and the fact that people make periodic calls, we find there is a ratio of around 100 MCP Control messages for each Tool Call.

Some clients also send requests that don't make sense for our Stateless, Direct Response configuration - for example Pings, Cancellations or attempts to list Resources (which isn't a capability we presently advertise).

The first week of July 2025 saw an astonishing 164 different Clients accessing our Server. Interestingly, one of the most popular tools is mcp-remote. Approximately half of all Clients use it as a bridge to connect to our remote server.

MCP is rapidly evolving, and we're excited about what has already been achieved across Chat Applications, IDEs, Agents and MCP Servers over the last few months.

We can already see how powerful integrating the Hugging Face Hub has been and support for Gradio Spaces now makes it possible for LLMs to be easily extended with the latest Machine Learning applications.

Here are some great examples of things people have been doing with our MCP Server so far:.

We hope that this post has provided insights to the decisions that need to be made building Remote MCP Servers, and encourage you to try some of the examples in your favourite MCP Client.

Take a look at our Open Source MCP Server, and try some of the different transport options with your Client, or open an Concern or Pull Request to make improvements or suggest new functionality.

Let us know your thoughts, feedback and questions on this discussion thread.
