A upcoming leak suggests that Samsung is preparing to copy the iPhone’s Dynamic Island feature in the not-too-distant future, to an extent that not many other Android brands have even done thus far.

Copying the Dynamic Island was briefly like a rite of passage for some Android brands, with many wasting almost no time in delivering their own version of the feature. But, on many of those devices, it’s a surface-level ripoff at best. The feature is primarily limited to music apps and timers, rarely working with any third-party apps in meaningful ways. Android has a built-in feature similar to Apple’s but not in the same styling.

Samsung is now preparing its own version of the Dynamic Island, and it seems this one has a bit more meat on its bones.

SamMobile on Twitter/X posted a video and two still images of what appears to be a Dynamic Island clone coming to Galaxy devices. It’s mentioned as potentially coming to the Galaxy S27 series (so, One UI 9.5) and being called “Moment Effects.” A portion of the software explicitly mentions integration with Google Sports, the leak claims, while it seems Samsung is using Live Notifications here, which already support a number of third-party apps.

The kicker from a UX perspective is that Samsung’s interpretation allows you to swipe between activities, similar to Apple, but the core premise is similar with the island showing around the selfie camera cutout.

When this feature might surface does remain unclear, but a One UI 9.5 debut would make plenty of sense. That update is in beta now and due to launch on the Galaxy S27 series early next year.

What do you think of Samsung’s alleged Dynamic Island clone? Personally, I’m on board as long as it proves useful, and it seems to be on the right track compared to most other copycats.

Your accessibility check in CI is green. axe-core ran, zero violations, and the badge in the README looks great. Your site can still fail WCAG 2.2.

Sources indicate that that isn't a bug in axe. WCAG 2.2 became a W3C Recommendation in October 2023. It added nine success criteria and dropped one (4.1.1 Parsing), and most of the upcoming ones can't be judged by reading the DOM. Deque mentioned as much when it shipped the first WCAG 2.2 support in axe-core 4.5: the target-size rule would probably be the only new-criterion rule they added, because the others can't be automated without a lot of false positives.

So the rest is on you. This article covers the one criterion axe can check and three it can't (focus not obscured, dragging movements, accessible authentication), with Playwright tests you can drop into a project. I ran all of them against a small test page that fails every criterion on purpose, and against a fixed version of the same page. If you want a plain-language rundown of every change first, WCAG 2.2 vs 2.1 goes through them. Here I only care about what you can put in a pipeline.

Level A and AA are what most contracts and laws point at, so those are the ones that matter first. The AAA criteria are still worth knowing about.

That's four AA criteria with something you can script, one of which axe already handles. The rest of this article goes through those four.

Recent findings suggest that the AA rule is smaller than most people expect: a pointer target should be at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, or sit far enough from its neighbours that a 24px circle centred on it wouldn't overlap another target or that target's own circle. There are exceptions, including inline links in a sentence, and targets whose size the browser controls.

It has been revealed that axe-core has a target-size rule for this. One catch: it isn't part of a default run. In my setup (axe-core 4.14.1 through @axe-core/playwright 4.14.0), a plain analyze() on the broken page reported nothing at all. The rule only showed up once I asked for it:.

On the broken page this lists the three 16px toolbar buttons by selector. On the fixed page, with 32px buttons, it passes. If you've been running axe for years and never seen a target-size result, this is why.

Some context on how common the problem is. In the scan data behind my last SitePoint article, 34.5% of the 1,025 sites had controls below a stricter 44px threshold. That is a tougher standard than the 24px that AA asks for, so don't read it as "a third of sites fail 2.5.8". Plenty of those would pass. But it does show how many production sites ship tiny controls.

If you'd like a quick look at one page before wiring anything up, browser tools such as axe DevTools, WAVE, or a WCAG checker will show the same thing.

axe can't test it, because you have to press Tab and look at where the browser scrolled. Two details caught me out building this:.

The check below samples a grid of points inside the visible part of the focused element and asks the browser what's on top at each one. If none of the points land on the element or its children, it's covered.

Sources indicate that on my broken page it reported nine hits: links hidden behind the footer going forward ("Section 4 link", "Section 10 link", "Section 16 link") and the toolbar buttons and a few links hidden behind the header coming back. The output names the element and the key, which is what you want when you're staring at a failed build.

The fix is one CSS rule, sized to your sticky elements:.

Industry observers note that that tells the browser to leave room when it scrolls a focused element into view. With it in place the same test passes.

Sources indicate that be aware of what this can't see: a modal that opens over the page, or a chat widget that only appears after a delay, will not show up unless your test opens or waits for them. Adrian Roselli's piece on 2.4.11 and adversarial conformance is worth reading for the awkward cases.

Anything you can do by dragging needs a way to do it with a single click or tap, unless dragging is essential. Sortable lists, sliders, kanban cards, file reorderers: all of them.

You can't prove a drag alternative works from a script. But you can catch the obvious mistake, which is a draggable item with no button anywhere near it:.

The limit is real. It only recognises the native draggable attribute. Libraries built on pointer events, such as dnd-kit, don't set it, so this test will walk right past them. If you use one of those, replace the selector with whatever your component renders, or add a test per drag component. Treat it as a tripwire for the common case, not a verdict.

The fix, in the fixed page, is a pair of "Move up" and "Move down" buttons on each item, each with an accessible name that notes which item it moves.

This dispatches a synthetic paste event and checks whether anything called preventDefault() on it. It catches the old onpaste="return false" trick, and it catches script-based blockers too. It does not tell you whether your login has a CAPTCHA that needs an alternative, or an emailed one-time code you must retype. Those need a person.

On a pull request, a plain GitHub Actions job is enough:.

According to recent reports, point PAGE_URL at a running preview, and run the tests against the pages that matter most: sign-in, checkout, anything with a sticky element. Don't try to crawl everything on the first pass. A test that fails for reasons nobody owns gets deleted within a month.

Four things I haven't tried to automate, and wouldn't:.

Automation will keep the regressions out. It won't tell you the work is finished. A green build and a conformant site are different things, and WCAG 2.2 widened the gap between them.

In a recent development, the tests and both test pages are small enough to read in one sitting. Copy what's useful, change the selectors, and keep the broken page around: it's a handy way to check that a test fails when it should.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TL;DR: ScreenEnv is a powerful Python library that lets you create isolated Ubuntu desktop environments in Docker containers for testing and deploying GUI Agents (aka Computer Use agents). With built-in support for the Model Context Protocol (MCP), it's never been easier to deploy desktop agents that can see, click, and interact with real applications.

Imagine you need to automate desktop tasks, test GUI applications, or build an AI agent that can interact with software. This used to require complex VM setups and brittle automation frameworks.

Industry observers note that screenEnv changes this by providing a sandboxed desktop environment that runs in a Docker container. Think of it as a complete virtual desktop session that your code can fully control - not just clicking buttons and typing text, but managing the entire desktop experience including launching applications, organizing windows, handling files, executing terminal commands, and recording the entire session.

ScreenEnv provides two complementary ways to integrate with your agents and backend systems, giving you flexibility to choose the approach that best fits your architecture:.

Perfect for custom agent frameworks, existing backends, or when you need fine-grained control:.

Ideal for AI systems that support the Model Context Protocol:.

This dual approach means ScreenEnv adapts to your existing infrastructure rather than forcing you to change your agent architecture.

screenenv natively supports smolagents, making it easy to build your own custom Desktop Agent for automation. Here’s how to create your own AI-powered Desktop Agent in just a few steps:.

Pick the backend VLM you want to power your agent.

Inherit from DesktopAgentBase and implement the _setup_desktop_tools method to build your own action space!

If you encounter acces denied docker error, you can try to run the agent with sudo -E python -m test.py or add your user to the docker group.

💡 For a comprehensive implementation, see this CustomDesktopAgent source on GitHub.

ScreenEnv aims to expand beyond Linux to support Android, macOS, and Windows, unlocking true cross-platform GUI automation. This will enable developers and researchers to build agents that generalize across environments with minimal setup.

These advancements pave the way for creating reproducible, sandboxed environments ideal for benchmarking and evaluation.

Asynchronous Robot Inference: Decoupling Action Prediction and Execution

📅 10 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1939 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • TL;DR Robotic policies are increasingly bulky, and predict chunks of future actions rather than a single next action.
  • Get started with async inference by following our tutorial.
  • It has been revealed that sequential inference (first) versus async inference (second).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TL;DR Robotic policies are increasingly bulky, and predict chunks of future actions rather than a single next action. This results in the robot being idle while awaiting new actions to perform, introducing noticeable lags at execution, and lacking responsiveness. Asynchronous inference tightens the control loop, removing lags at runtime and resulting in more adaptive control by decoupling action prediction from action execution. In this blog post, we cover the basics behind async inference, and how it can be used to improve the performance of robotic policies in the real-world.

Get started with async inference by following our tutorial.

It has been revealed that sequential inference (first) versus async inference (second). Allowing for replanning and a tighter control loop, async inference results in (1) attempts at recovery, and (2) a ~2x speedup in task completion. Sequential inference keeps acting out the current action chunk even after failure to grasp the object, while async inference can replan and act the newly introduced action chunk. Both setups use the same policy!

With async inference, we decouple action execution from action prediction. This is particularly relevant considering the tendency of currently popular models like [ACT], [OpenVLA], [PI0], and [SmolVLA] to be outputting chunks of actions at:t+Ha_{t:t+H}at:t+H​ rather than single actions ata_tat​ given an observation oto_tot​. Convince yourself of this by running all these models using LeRobot.

Using chunks sequentially results in (1) lags at runtime, impacting task execution time and (2) lack of responsiveness, due to acting widely open-loop. Asynchronous inference mitigates both these limitations by decoupling action prediction from action execution. We introduced asynchronous inference in SmolVLA, and found it to result in a ~2x speed-up in task completion time with comparable task success rate.

In particular, we design a 2-component system where policy inference and action execution are performed in two different processes, possibly on two different machines connected through the network:.

Communication between PolicyServer and RobotClient relies on gRPC, which guarantees ~5× faster performance than a comparable REST API. The result of all of this is a robot that never waits for inference.

Asynchronous inference, highlighting: (1) The client sending the first observation for inference, receiving the first chunk shortly after; (2) The client sending another observation for processing while it has not yet exhausted the current chunk; (3) The client receiving an updated action chunk, which it aggregates with the remainders of the one it was previously executing.

It has been revealed that suppose a policy π \pi π maps the current observation ot o_t ot​ to a sequence of H H H future actions. Formally, π:O  ↦  A,At=(at,at+1,…at+H)=π(ot)\pi : \mathcal{O} \;\mapsto\; \mathcal{A}, \mathbf{A}_t = \begin{pmatrix} a_{t}, & a_{t+1}, & \dots & a_{t+H} \end{pmatrix} = \pi(o_t)π:O↦A,At​=(at​,​at+1​,​…​at+H​​)=π(ot​).

A traditional control loop would therefore consist of the following steps:.

During step 2 the robot is idle. The latency grows with the model size (and models tend to be increasingly bulky over time), and can rapidly dominate interaction time (which is typically around 1/fps), as shown in the video below (coming from our Discord community 🤗):.

This directly results in (1) reduced performance in terms of task completion time---the robot needs to be waiting for the next action chunk to be computed---and (2) reduced responsiveness, due to (2.1) acting widely open-loop while actions are available and (2.2) complete idleness while waiting for the next action chunk.

(Left)Sequential inference with highlighted idle periods. (Right)Time to select an action showing spikes when inference is triggered due to local queue exhaustion (inference latency is around ~100ms---~3 frames at 30fps---using an ACT model on a 2021 MacBook Pro).

Our system removes the idle period by overlapping computation and execution:.

The key idea is that the robot already knows what to do for the next few timesteps, so it can keep moving while fresh actions are being computed on the server.

Asynchronous inference overlaps in time the execution of the current action chunk with the computation of the next one, by decoupling these two processes, possibly running them on entirely distinct machines connected through the network.

This results in a tighter control loop, and a robot that never waits for inference. In turn, this results in ~2x speedup in task completion time with comparable task success rate, and more adaptive control coming from a tighter loop (see video below).

Because gRPC is HTTP/2-based and uses protocol buffers, it achieves low-latency binary messaging and bidirectional streams out of the box, which in turn helps us maintain a tighter control loop and sub-100ms round-trip latency (on our local network, and hosting SmolVLA on a NVIDIA RTX 4090).

Sources indicate that the RobotClient runs on-board, and streams observations to the PolicyServer through gRPC. The PolicyServer prepares the observations received for inference, and sends back to the RobotClient an action chunk.

From the client's perspective, observations are streamed to the server according to the local queue status. Incoming chunks are aggregated on overlapping portions with the at the moment available action queue.

The RobotClient maintains a local action queue and follows a simple yet effective strategy: send a latest observation when the queue length drops below a configurable threshold (\(g\) in the SmolVLA paper, chunk_size_threshold in the code). This threshold value, expressed as a fraction of the maximum chunk size, acts as a trigger condition that balances computational load with responsiveness.

The client streams observations to the server, according to the local queue status.

From the client's perspective, the process unfolds as follows:.

Recent findings suggest that queue monitoring: The client continuously monitors its action queue length against a chunk size threshold parameter. When the queue drops below this threshold, it signals that a fresh observation should be sent for processing.

It has been revealed that observation streaming: Once the threshold condition is met, the client captures the current observation and streams it to the PolicyServer via gRPC. Crucially, observations are streamed rather than being sent via a unary RPC because they typically exceed the maximum message size of 4MB (multiple camera captures at high resolution result in this).

In a recent development, action chunk aggregation: When a newly introduced action chunk arrives from the server, the client merges it with any remaining actions in the current queue over the overlapping portion. This is where custom aggregators come into play, handling overlapping sections between the current and incoming chunks differently. As of now, we support flexibly aggregation between the chunks via the specification of a custom aggregate_fn(chunk1: torch.Tensor, chunk2: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor function, which is called for each overlapping timestep and can be user-provided. The overlapping portions (shown in light blue in the diagram) require careful handling. We can design different aggregation strategies:.

This system is highly configurable, as the chunk size threshold can be tuned based on network latency, model inference time, and desired responsiveness. A lower threshold means more frequent updates (and higher computational cost), while a higher threshold reduces communication overhead at the expense of potential queue starvation. Lastly, we typically receive actions from PolicyServer in a thread, and perform them in another one. This keeps the client listening for incoming chunks in a separate thread, without blocking execution and always consuming the current chunk until a new one becomes fully available.

According to recent reports, upon receiving observations from the RobotClient, the PolicyServer receives observations from the RobotClient, and performs the necessary observation cleaning to make received observations ready for inference. This process is illustrated in the image below:.

The observation cleaning pipeline running on the server, highlighting the three main steps related to (1) Keys matching (2) Preprocessing and (3) Preparation for inference.

Recent findings suggest that once the observation has been prepared, it is compared with the last observation used for inference. This avoids collapsing into a loop whereby very similar observations are processed, thus triggering unnecessary inference and similar actions being executed (which in turn, result in very similar observations being processed again). We compare observations in terms of their joint-space similarity, which provides us an approximate and quick way of measuring changes in the robot. Clearly, this metric is not adaptive to dynamic changes in the environment (an object changing its position, or disturbances being applied), but we found it to be a good trade-off for the majority of the cases, and to be very effective in avoiding unnecessary inference and state collapse. Critically, the RobotClient retains control over whether a given observation must be processed, to avoid deadlocks. Observations sent by the client and tagged with must_go=True are processed regardless of the similarity metric.

The policy workflow, in which incoming observations are compared to the last one used for inference, and processed only if different enough, or `must_go`.

In a recent development, lastly, to ensure the PolicyServer always processes the latest available observation, we block incoming observations until the previous one has been successfully processed. In this, we leverage queues on the PolicyServer to ensure incoming observations are not enqueued until the server is ready to process them (see below).

The client pings the server every 1/fps seconds, but observations are not enqueued for processing until the previous one has been successfully processed.

Recent findings suggest that A short clip can help a project in different ways. It can show an idea you have not filmed, put an existing design in motion, or give an announcement something to look at. The same approach will not work if the clip needs to demonstrate a real feature or show exactly what happened. Before choosing a generator, decide what the viewer needs to learn from the shot.

This article uses Kling 4.0 as a worked example, but the decision process applies to any AI video generator. It covers how these tools turn prompts and images into video, how Kling 4.0 and a few alternatives differ, how to choose a starting mode, how to add exact text and branding outside the generated clip with a short ffmpeg script, and when real footage is the better choice. Feature details come from each vendor’s own pages at the time of writing and change often, so confirm current terms before you plan a production.

It has been revealed that ● Generated video is best for imagined shots. It suits concepts, backgrounds and early explorations, not instructions or faithful records.

● Your starting material decides the mode. A written idea, a reference image or a pair of opening and closing frames each call for a different input.

It has been revealed that ● Keep exact wording out of the generated clip. Titles, dates and logos belong on separate layers in an editor.

● Tools differ on control, cost and licensing. Compare inputs, length, resolution, credits and terms before you commit.

According to recent reports, ● Always review. Watch the whole clip at its final size and check it against the real product or design.

Most current systems extend diffusion models across time. A model learns to turn noise into a coherent set of frames guided by a prompt, and sometimes by an image or a clip. The research paper Video Diffusion Models describes this extension from images to video. The practical consequences are easy to observe.

Industry observers note that ● The prompt describes change over time. One visible change and one camera instruction usually work better than a long list of actions.

According to recent reports, ● Reference material steers but does not lock. A picture can suggest shape and colour without guaranteeing an exact match.

In a recent development, ● Longer clips give more room for drift. Faces, logos and fine text are the first things to change between frames.

It has been revealed that ● Cost grows with length and resolution. Most hosted tools charge credits per second, so short previews are cheaper than full shots.

Industry observers note that if you only have an idea, start with text. For a short announcement, you might ask for a band of light to move across a wall of coloured tiles. No one needs to recognise a particular wall, so the model can decide how it looks. Give it one visible change and a clear view of the subject. A prompt such as Soft morning light travels slowly across a wall of blue ceramic tiles. Fixed camera, no lettering is enough to see whether the idea works.

If you already have an illustration or a photo, reference mode gives you another starting point. Suppose you want a short concept clip for a desk accessory that only exists as a drawing. The picture can show the general shape and colour while the prompt describes the view you want. A video reference can help when it is the motion that is hard to explain, such as a slow camera slide. Say what each asset is meant to guide, and do not add a clip just because you have one.

Use keyframes when a particular view matters at a particular moment. Start with an opening image. If a short reveal also needs to end with the object facing forward, add an ending image to show that view. That is different from a reference image that mainly highlights what the object looks like. Neither method guarantees an exact match, so check the result rather than assuming the uploaded picture has locked the design.

According to recent reports, no single tool fits every project. The table summarizes what each option’s own page states, and “not stated” means the page did not say, not that the feature is absent.

Recent findings suggest that reading the table: hosted studios such as the one on JXP are the quickest way to test an idea and need no setup, but you pay per second and work within their supported inputs. Runway positions its models for motion quality and prompt following, while Google’s Gemini API video documentation suits teams building generation into their own products. The Diffusers video guide covers open-source pipelines for developers who want local control and are ready to manage GPUs and licences.

Trying an idea before making it. An illustrator might want to see how an imagined landscape feels when the light changes. A quick clip gives the team something to discuss: is the change visible, and does it happen at the right pace? It does not need to be the final animation to answer those questions.

Sources indicate that showing a product concept. A rotating view or a slow camera move can help people discuss how a design might be presented. It is useful early, when the shape and lighting are still being explored. Once the clip represents a product someone can buy, the standard changes. If a port moves or a button appears that the real product does not have, it is the wrong clip for that job.

In a recent development, making a short visual for a post. A few seconds of moving colour can give an event announcement or a project update a distinctive opening. Put the name, date and other exact wording in your editor so they are readable and easy to change. The background only needs to support the message. If it competes with the text, use less movement or keep the background still.

Sources indicate that generated video is unreliable at lettering, so add titles in an editor or with a script. The command below overlays a title on a generated background and then checks the file properties. It assumes you already have a clip named background.mp4 and ffmpeg installed.

-vf "drawtext=text='Launch Night | 12 March':fontcolor=white:fontsize=64:x=(w-text_w)/2:y=(h-text_h)/2:box=1:boxcolor=black@0.35:boxborderw=24" \.

-c:v libx264 -pix_fmt yuv420p -an announcement.mp4.

ffprobe -v error -select_streams v:0 \.

-show_entries stream=width,height,r_frame_rate,duration \.

-of default=noprint_wrappers=1 announcement.mp4.

Recent findings suggest that because the text lives in the command, you can reuse the same background for three events by changing one string. The font may need to be set with a fontfile option on some systems. This is the practical version of keeping the moving background in one file and the editable details in another.

Industry observers note that if people will follow the clip as instructions, use real footage or a screen recording for the steps. A convincing shot of an app is not proof that a button is in the right place. A generated close-up of a product is not a reliable way to show how its parts fit. You can still use an imagined opening, but make the switch to the real demonstration clear.

Think about revisions, too. If your team expects to adjust the same title, logo or date every week, put those elements on separate layers in an editor. And if the only movement you need is a slow zoom on an approved picture, apply that zoom directly. There is no reason to risk changing the picture when a simple edit will do.

According to recent reports, this matters when someone else will maintain the video. A reusable announcement template is easier to hand over if the moving background is one file and the event details are editable. If the team likes the movement but needs three versions with different dates, they can reuse the same clip. If every change calls for a latest generation, the time you saved on the first version may disappear on the second.

Sources indicate that the Kling 4.0 video generator on JXP currently offers 720p and 1080p settings and clip lengths from 3 to 30 seconds. According to its page, reference mode accepts up to 10 images and 5 videos, keyframe mode takes a first frame, middle frames and an optional last frame, and credits are charged per second with a higher rate at 1080p. For a first attempt, choose the frame shape you plan to use and make the clip only as long as it needs to be. Check the displayed credit cost before generating, because a short preview can tell you whether the direction works before you spend on a longer shot.

Decide what a good result looks like before you generate it. For the tile background, you need to see the light move without distracting from the words you will add. For a product concept, check whether the shape stays recognisable as the viewpoint changes. Watch the whole clip at the size the audience will see it. If the shot misses the point, revise one thing at a time: the motion, the framing or the source image.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Over the past month, Gemini 4 Argon and Gemini 4 Carbon brought frontier physical reasoning to robotics: understanding 3D scenes, reconstructing real environments in simulation, practicing tasks in sim before running them on hardware, and directly controlling robot arms from camera images.
  • Recent findings suggest that to help developers put Hydrogen to work, today we're launching the Robotics plugin on Google Antigravity: a set of skills for hardware onboarding, simulation and robot control turning Antigravity into a one-stop robotics workbench.
  • Gemini 4 Argon and Carbon showed that a general model can drive a robot arm directly, and Gemini 4 Hydrogen preserves that ability.

Over the past month, Gemini 4 Argon and Gemini 4 Carbon brought frontier physical reasoning to robotics: understanding 3D scenes, reconstructing real environments in simulation, practicing tasks in sim before running them on hardware, and directly controlling robot arms from camera images. Last week, we introduced Gemini 4 Hydrogen, which brings strong spatial and embodied reasoning to a much faster model built for speed and efficiency.

Recent findings suggest that to help developers put Hydrogen to work, today we're launching the Robotics plugin on Google Antigravity: a set of skills for hardware onboarding, simulation and robot control turning Antigravity into a one-stop robotics workbench. Together, they enable a developer to go from a robot in a box to one that can perform a working application in an afternoon. To install the plugin, open Antigravity, go to Customizations and search for Robotics on the Build With Google shelf.

Gemini 4 Argon and Carbon showed that a general model can drive a robot arm directly, and Gemini 4 Hydrogen preserves that ability. Give it a goal in plain language and a camera view, and it prepares the task, writes and runs the control code, and keeps adjusting until the job is done. On the Artificial Analysis Robotics 0.1 benchmark, Gemini 4 Hydrogen controls a real 6-axis arm through eight everyday tabletop tasks, from pouring a drink to packing blocks into a box. Hydrogen scores 58, similar to Argon at a lower cost per token.

In a recent development, hydrogen brings the specialized skills of our Gemini Robotics ER 2 (Embodied Reasoning) models into the core Gemini 4 model series, and it beats them on nearly every axis. On the public ERQA benchmark, Hydrogen outperforms Gemini Robotics ER 2 on spatial reasoning tasks such as multi-view correspondence and 3D trajectory reasoning. For developers using Gemini Robotics ER 2 today, we recommend trying out Gemini 4 Hydrogen for these workloads.

Kimina-Prover: Applying Test-time RL Search on Large Formal Reasoning Models

📅 10 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2412 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We're excited to announce the release of Kimina-Prover-72B, our state-of-the-art theorem proving model trained with the Kimi k1.5[1] RL pipeline based on Qwen2.5-72B [2].
  • Test-Time Reinforcement Learning Search: A trainable agentic proving framework that enables the model to recursively discover, combine and apply multiple lemmas to construct complex proofs, building on a novel lemma-enabled pattern.
  • Error-Fixing Capability: Kimina-Prover can read and interpret Lean’s error messages and propose targeted fixes, demonstrating significantly higher sample efficiency compared to regenerating proofs from scratch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We're excited to announce the release of Kimina-Prover-72B, our state-of-the-art theorem proving model trained with the Kimi k1.5[1] RL pipeline based on Qwen2.5-72B [2]. Alongside it, we are also releasing two distilled variants: Kimina-Prover-Distill-8B and 1.7B (based on Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-1.7B[3] respectively).

Test-Time Reinforcement Learning Search: A trainable agentic proving framework that enables the model to recursively discover, combine and apply multiple lemmas to construct complex proofs, building on a novel lemma-enabled pattern.

Error-Fixing Capability: Kimina-Prover can read and interpret Lean’s error messages and propose targeted fixes, demonstrating significantly higher sample efficiency compared to regenerating proofs from scratch.

These advancements enable Kimina-Prover to solve challenging mathematical problems and surpass prior methods. As shown in Figure 1, on the widely used miniF2F benchmark, Kimina-Prover achieves a state-of-the-art pass rate of 92.2%.

Industry observers note that we focus on automated theorem proving (ATP) in the Lean 4 language, aiming to automate the construction of formal mathematical proofs. Recent advances in neural theorem proving have significantly improved the ability of AI systems to assist with or automate this process. Notable progress includes AlphaProof[4] from Google DeepMind, which demonstrated strong performance on problems at the level of the International Mathematical Olympiad. Open-source systems such as DeepSeek-Prover-V2[5], which incorporates reinforcement learning, have also achieved state-of-the-art results. In addition, neuro-symbolic agentic approaches like DSP+[6] have shown that competitive performance is possible without large-scale training by leveraging off-the-shelf models in a modular framework.

It has been revealed that our earlier work of Kimina-Prover Preview[7] introduced a large language model for formal theorem proving in Lean, establishing a new performance baseline on the miniF2F benchmark. Trained with a large-scale reinforcement learning pipeline, the model adopted a reasoning-driven exploration paradigm and demonstrated that larger models can serve as stronger formal reasoners. Its structured reasoning pattern enabled efficient proof search and emulated human-like problem-solving strategies.

Industry observers note that following this initial success, we continued to improve the model through further iterations of reinforcement learning. However, single-step reasoning remains insufficient for solving complex problems that require long, multi-stage proofs. To address this limitation, we introduce the Test-Time Reinforcement Learning (TTRL) search framework, which enables the model to discover, combine, and reuse multiple intermediate lemmas autonomously. This framework supports deeper, long-horizon reasoning by decomposing hard problems into reusable subcomponents.

Recent findings suggest that A key ingredient of TTRL search is the lemma-enabled pattern, which allows the model to identify and apply intermediate lemmas as part of its proof construction process. This structured reuse of intermediate results significantly expands the model’s problem-solving capability beyond single-step generation.

In a recent development, to further enhance robustness, we also integrate an error-fixing mechanism that interprets Lean’s error messages and proposes targeted corrections. This allows the model to refine its outputs through iterative feedback, improving proof reliability and overall sample efficiency.

According to recent reports, as the combination of the proposed techniques results in significant improvements in formal theorem proving performance. On the miniF2F benchmark, Kimina-Prover achieves a pass rate of 84.0% with pass@32 and 86.4% with the addition of a single round of error correction. With pass@1024, the pass rate reaches 87.7%. Applying the full Test-Time Reinforcement Learning (TTRL) search framework yields a final pass rate of 92.2%, with an estimated pass upper bound of approximately 42,000. However, this pass budget can be substantially optimized in future versions, as a large portion of the current sampling is spent on proving unhelpful or redundant lemmas.

Sources indicate that notably, these results indicate a shift in the scaling behavior of the prover. While earlier versions exhibited approximately linear improvements in log scale with increasing sampling budget, the current system highlights diminishing returns beyond pass@1024. This suggests that further gains are less dependent on increased sampling and instead require more sophisticated search strategies, such as those introduced by TTRL.

In a recent development, the lemma-enabled pattern is designed to equip the model with the ability to identify and utilize useful lemmas provided in the input. To support this capability, during reinforcement learning (RL) training, a random subset of one to three formal lemmas is prepended to the problem context, exposing the prover to potentially useful intermediate results that can aid in constructing the final proof. These lemmas are prepared through a two-step pipeline: (1) a general-purpose LLM generates candidate lemmas in natural language; (2) these are then translated into formal statements using our Kimina-Autoformalizer-7b.

Initial observations revealed that the model had a low tendency to incorporate the provided lemmas. To address this, we introduced a preference-based reward shaping strategy within the RL framework. When a theorem could be proven through multiple trajectories, solutions that successfully leveraged a provided lemma were assigned a higher reward, while those that did not were penalized. This approach proved effective, increasing the lemma utilization rate to a stable 30–40% after training. Importantly, this method not only encouraged lemma usage but also promoted selectivity: the model learned to apply lemmas strategically when they were useful, while ignoring irrelevant ones, demonstrating more efficient and human-like reasoning behavior.

The lemma-enabled pattern allowed the model to incorporate pre-generated lemmas as intermediate steps in constructing proofs. However, we observed that randomly sampling and inserting lemmas was insufficient for solving complex problems requiring highly structured and deeply nested reasoning. To address this limitation, we developed the Test-Time Reinforcement Learning Search framework—a trainable, agentic approach that systematically organizes, filters, and composes a large set of candidate lemmas to build complete proofs. This framework transitions the process from random exploration to a more strategic, goal-directed search.

According to recent reports, as illustrated in Figure 2, we define the search scope of each problem as the problem itself along with its associated candidate lemmas. TTRL Search tracks a lemma utilization score within each search scope to measure how frequently and effectively each lemma contributes to the final proof. At the beginning of each RL training iteration, for each problem (i.e., search scope), we construct K = 10 input variants by prepending different combinations of lemmas. To balance exploration and exploitation, 60% of the inputs are built using the top-ranking lemmas—those with the highest utilization scores—focusing the model on the most promising proof paths. The remaining 40% are formed by including these top lemmas alongside one to four randomly selected additional lemmas, encouraging exploration of novel and potentially useful lemma combinations.

To ensure quality, a filtering mechanism prunes lemmas that consistently fail to contribute meaningfully: any lemma that fails to achieve a utilization score of at least τ=0.10 after 50 insertion attempts is removed from the search pool.

A key feature of TTRL is its recursive search mechanism. The search scope is not limited to the original theorem but is also maintained for each lemma, allowing the framework to recursively decompose the problem into smaller subproblems. A parallel sublemma generation process runs throughout, and whenever a theorem or lemma fails to find a proof after N = 128 attempts, upcoming candidate sublemmas are generated. This recursive strategy enables test-time scaling of reasoning depth, significantly extending the model’s effective problem-solving capability.

Industry observers note that to maintain logical soundness, we address a failure mode wherein incorrectly formalized lemmas could lead to trivial or invalid proofs. In such cases, the model may exploit inconsistencies to construct seemingly valid but unsound solutions. To prevent this, we introduce a negation proving process: for each newly generated lemma, we attempt to prove its logical negation. If the negated statement is provable, it indicates that the original lemma is logically inconsistent and is immediately discarded. This step ensures the reliability and soundness of the overall proof construction process.

A critical limitation of recent advanced theorem proving models is their lack of the ability to correct proofs based on feedback from the proof assistant—capabilities that human users routinely leverage. To address this gap, we developed a dedicated framework to integrate error-fixing capabilities into Kimina-Prover.

In a recent development, SFT Data Generation for Error Correction. General-purpose large language models exhibit a low success rate when interpreting Lean’s error messages and proposing valid corrections. To overcome this, we constructed a specialized Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) dataset tailored for error correction. This dataset consists of triplets in the form of (incorrect proof, Lean feedback, correct proof). To enrich the supervision signal, we prompted Claude 3.7 sonnet[8] to synthesize step-by-step reasoning chains explaining how the incorrect proof can be transformed into the correct one using the provided feedback. The result is a high-quality dataset that includes not only the initial and corrected proofs but also the intermediate reasoning, facilitating more effective learning.

Industry observers note that batched Failure Replay Strategy. Integrating error correction directly into the reinforcement learning (RL) loop initially proved ineffective due to the low success rate (~1%) of the SFT model in fixing errors, resulting in sparse rewards and unstable training. To address this, we designed the Batched Failure Replay strategy. Rather than attempting to correct errors immediately during an RL iteration, all failed proof attempts from iteration N are collected. In the subsequent iteration N+1, the training batch is composed of a fixed-size union of these prior failures (e.g., 500 samples) and standard problems from the prompt set (e.g., another 500 samples). This ensures consistent and high-volume exposure to error correction tasks in each training step, enabling the model to gradually learn effective error-handling behaviors in a stable and data-efficient manner.

Recent findings suggest that this training approach led to measurable improvements in the model’s ability to recover from failure. The model advanced from correcting basic syntax errors to resolving complex logical mistakes and, eventually, discovering alternative proof strategies when initial attempts failed. Crucially, this capability improved sample efficiency. As shown in Table 2, we compared different strategies under fixed computational budgets. The 16+16 attempt-and-fix strategy—consisting of 16 initial proof attempts, each followed by one error-fixing attempt—achieved a success rate of 35.6%, outperforming the 32×1 brute-force baseline, which reached 28.8% with 32 independent attempts. Further increasing the sample budget to 32+32 with error correction yielded a success rate of 44.1%. These results demonstrate that enabling the model to correct its own errors is a more efficient use of computational resources than repeated trial-and-error.

In addition to our core TTRL search and Error fixing, we developed several other novel techniques to enhance the model's learning process and problem-solving capabilities.

Prompt Set Curation and Iteration. Effective data curation is critical for reinforcement learning (RL) efficiency. Our initial prompt set of over 300K problems was refined to a competition-focused subset of approximately 90K, with an emphasis on problems from sources such as the olympiads-ref subset of NuminaMath 1.5[9]. During RL, we applied dynamic filtering: problems with consistently high success rates were removed to maintain challenge, while persistently difficult problems were decomposed into simpler subproblems or variations using a general-purpose LLM. The final prompt set combines auto-formalized statements for broad coverage, human-annotated problems for quality, and augmented variations for targeted skill development. The curated prompt set will be open-sourced.

Industry observers note that continuous Pre-training on Lean Data. To address the limited Lean proficiency in most base models, we applied Continuous Pre-training (CPT). A 6-billion-token CPT dataset was constructed from multiple sources: 260M tokens from online platforms such as GitHub, 5.5B tokens of compiler-validated rollout data from our RL pipeline, and additional structured data in state–tactic–state and state–tactic–error formats to enhance diversity. These structured data supplements the base model with additional domain knowledge.

According to recent reports, random Proof Cut Data Augmentation. To better utilize high-quality, human-annotated proofs that lack intermediate reasoning steps, we developed the Random Proof Cut technique. This method augments such data using two variations:.

This strategy allows the model to learn how to extend existing lines of reasoning and to fill in logical gaps, effectively integrating human-generated content into the training process.

Non-proof Problem Solving. Many problems are presented in the form of requiring a final answer, which cannot be naturally framed as a traditional proof task. Inspired by the CombiBench[10] evaluation methodology, we introduced a capability for non-proof problem solving to unify answer generation with proof construction. In this setting, the model is given a problem with the final answer field left blank. It performs a two-stage process within a single inference: it first deduces the correct answer and then generates a complete formal proof to justify that answer. This approach ensures the model’s reasoning is explicitly conditioned on reaching the correct solution.

It has been revealed that here we provide some proof cases found by our newest Kimina-prover model. The complete list of solved miniF2F problems is available on GitHub.

According to recent reports, the system recursively decomposed the problem into four layers of lemmas using a TTRL search approach, ultimately generating a 520-line formal proof. During this recursive proving process, initially, only one lemma, sum_cexp_div_pow_ne_zero, remained to be solved. While this conclusion seems straightforward to prove informally, it would still require a lot of steps to prove it rigorously in Lean 4. Our system recursively generated two extra layers of lemmas and obtained a 260-line formal proof for sum_cexp_div_pow_ne_zero. This proof is valid under Mathlib v4.15.

It has been revealed that in the following example, the initial proof timed out because directly applying simp to ((Real.sqrt 3 / 2 : ℂ) + (1 / 2) * Complex.I) ^ 12 resulted in excessive search complexity. Breaking down the proof by step-by-step calculating intermediate powers like $z^3$, then $z^6$, and finally $z^{12}$ significantly reduced the computational burden on the compiler.

If you'd like to cite Kimina-Prover, please feel free to reference our preview paper for now. A full paper is currently in preparation and will be available soon.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, in January of this year, Hugging Face's Xet Team deployed a newly introduced storage backend, and shortly after shifted ~6% of Hub downloads through the infrastructure. This represented a significant milestone, but it was just the beginning. In 6 months, 500,000 repositories holding 20 PB joined the move to Xet as the Hub outgrows Git LFS and transitions to a storage system that scales with the workloads of AI builders.

Today, more than 1 million people on the Hub are using Xet. In May, it became the default on the Hub for latest customers and organizations. With only a few dozen GitHub concerns, forum threads, and Discord messages, this is perhaps the quietest migration of this magnitude.

How? For one, the team came prepared with years of experience building and supporting the content addressed store (CAS) and Rust client that provide the system's foundation. Without these pieces, Git LFS may still be the future on the Hub. However, the unsung heroes of this migration are:.

Together, these components have allowed us to aggressively migrate PBs in the span of days without worrying about the impact to the Hub or the community. They're giving us the peace of mind to move even faster in the coming weeks and months (skip to the end 👇 to see what's coming).

In the early days of planning the migration to Xet, we made a few key design decisions:.

Driven by our commitment to the community, these seemingly straightforward decisions had significant implications. Most importantly, we did not believe owners and teams should have to immediately alter their workflow or download a newly introduced client to interact with Xet-enabled repositories.

If you have a Xet-aware client (e.g., hf-xet, the Xet integration with huggingface_hub), uploads and downloads pass through the entire Xet stack. The client either breaks up files into chunks using content defined chunking while uploading, or requests file reconstruction information when downloading. On upload, chunks are passed to CAS and stored in S3. During downloads, CAS provides the chunk ranges the client needs to request from S3 to reconstruct the file locally.

Sources indicate that for older versions of huggingface_hub or huggingface.js, which do not support chunk-based file transfers, you can still download and upload to Xet repos, but these bytes take a different route. When a Xet-backed file is requested from the Hub along the resolve endpoint, the Git LFS Bridge constructs and returns a single presigned URL, mimicking the LFS protocol. The Bridge then does the work of reconstructing the file from the content held in S3 and returns it to the requester.

In a recent development, to see this in action, right click on the image above and open it in a new tab. The URL redirects from https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/blog/migrating-the-hub-to-xet/bridge.png to one that begins with https://cas-bridge.xethub.hf.co/xet-bridge-us/.... You can also use curl -vL on the same URL to see the redirects in your terminal.

Meanwhile, when a non-Xet-aware client uploads a file, it is sent first to LFS storage then migrated to Xet. This “background migration process,” only briefly mentioned in our docs, powers both the migrations to Xet and upload backward compatibility. It is behind the migration of well over a dozen PBs of models and datasets and is keeping 500,000 repos in sync with Xet storage all without missing a beat.

According to recent reports, every time a file needs to be migrated from LFS to Xet, a webhook is triggered, pushing the event to a distributed queue where it is processed by an orchestrator. The orchestrator:.

These migration workers then pick up the jobs and each pod:.

In April, we tested this system's limits by reaching out to bartowski and asking if they wanted to test out Xet. With nearly 500 TB across 2,000 repos, bartowski's migration uncovered a few weak links:.

Sources indicate that fixing this three-headed monster meant touching every layer - patching xet-core, resizing CAS, and beefing up the worker node specs. Fortunately, bartowski was game to work with us while every repo made its way to Xet. These same lessons powered the moves of the biggest storage people on the Hub like RichardErkhov (1.7PB and 25,000 repos) and mradermacher (6.1PB and 42,000 repos 🤯).

CAS throughput, meanwhile, has grown by an order of magnitude between the first and latest large-scale migrations:.

When we began replacing LFS, we had two goals in mind:.

Designing with our initial constraints and these goals allowed us to:.

It has been revealed that instead of waiting for all upload paths to become Xet-aware, forcing a hard cut-over, or pushing the community to adopt a specific workflow, we could begin migrating the Hub to Xet immediately with minimal user impact. In short, let teams keep their workflows and organically transition to Xet with infrastructure supporting the long-term goal of a unified storage system.

In January and February, we onboarded power people to provide feedback and pressure-test the infrastructure. To get community feedback, we launched a waitlist to preview Xet-enabled repositories. Soon after, Xet became the default for new users on the Hub.

We now support some of the largest creators on the Hub (Meta Llama, Google, OpenAI, and Qwen) while the community keeps working uninterrupted.

Starting this month, we're bringing Xet to everyone. Watch for an email providing access to Xet and once you have it, update to the latest huggingface_hub (pip install -U huggingface_hub) to unlock faster transfers right away. This will also mean:.

If you upload or download from the Hub using your browser or use Git, that's fine. Chunk-based support for both is coming soon. In the meantime use whichever workflow you already have; no restrictions.

According to recent reports, next up: open-sourcing the Xet protocol and the entire infrastructure stack. The future of storing and moving bytes that scale to AI workloads is on the Hub, and we're aiming to bring it to everyone.

If you have any questions, drop us a line in the comments 👇, open a discussion on the Xet team page.

Not a dumb question at all. The Hub reports storage based on the logical size of each fresh object; what you're seeing is expected.

For the use-case that you're describing, Xet still provides faster file transfers as there is less to push and pull, so changes finish faster and uses less bandwidth/compute.

Sources indicate that this enables and strengthens our commitment to provide free public storage to the open source community. Of course, we're always evaluating ways to surface this transparently and support the community, so let me know if any of this is confusing.

For example if people are paying for extra private storage, and their storage is being counted “full size” against limits whilst being deduplicated against the rest of the hub and therefore a fraction of that in reality, is that fair? AI companions are the most demanding consumer use of large language models right now. A coding assistant can forget your last message and still be useful. A companion that forgets your name, your running story, or the plan you made last Tuesday has failed at its one job. On top of that, owners now expect voice calls that feel like a phone conversation, not a walkie-talkie exchange with a five-second pause.

Industry observers note that three engineering problems decide whether a companion app works: how much of the conversation fits in the model's context window, what the app remembers once the window fills up, and how fast the voice pipeline answers. Here is how consumer companions handle each one, with real tier and pricing examples, and what developers can take from their designs for their own products.

In a recent development, most LLM products are judged on single answers. Companions are judged on continuity. That creates pressure in three places at once:.

Every consumer companion is a different set of trade-offs across those three constraints, and the trade-offs are increasingly how the apps are priced.

The context window is the total number of tokens the model can see when it writes the next reply. In a companion app, that budget is spent before the user says anything:.

When the chat log outgrows what is left, the oldest messages fall out. The user experiences this as the companion "forgetting" mid-conversation. This is why context size is now a headline spec in the category, and a paid feature. SpicyChat AI, for example, gives free accounts a 4K context window, then scales memory to 8K on its $19.95/mo tier and 32K on its $29.95/mo tier. Janitor AI runs about 9K of context on its own JanitorLLM. Independent uncensored AI chat benchmarks record these context sizes alongside refusal behavior and pricing, because context length predicts how long a roleplay stays coherent better than any marketing claim.

According to recent reports, some apps sell memory in messages rather than tokens. Fantasy GF's pricing page lists a 60-message base "smart memory" and 5x that, 300 messages, on its Ultra plan. Others sell it as a memory multiplier on higher subscription tiers. The pattern is consistent across the category: memory depth is the upgrade lever, not the model itself.

According to recent reports, no consumer app keeps an entire relationship in the prompt. Persistent memory is a separate system that writes to storage and reads back into the context window on each turn. In practice it has three layers:.

Industry observers note that the differences owners notice are usually retention policies, not algorithms. Crushon AI's own subscription docs say free-plan chat history is deleted after 7 days of inactivity, while paid plans keep it for the membership period. Paid tiers across the category commonly promise that memories never expire. There is also a security angle worth stating plainly: companion chat logs are among the most sensitive data a consumer product can hold. A 2024 breach at Muah.ai, first reported by 404 Media, exposed roughly 1.9 million users' email addresses together with their private prompts. Any app that builds persistent memory is also building a liability, and developers copying the pattern should treat the memory store as the most protected part of the system.

Industry observers note that A voice call in a companion app is three models chained together: speech-to-text, the LLM, and text-to-speech. Run them strictly in sequence and a single reply can take several seconds, which reads as dead air. The apps that feel fast attack each stage the same way:.

It has been revealed that with every stage streaming, time-to-first-audio can land close to a second on a good connection, which is roughly the threshold where a conversation stops feeling laggy. Voice is also expensive to run - three model calls instead of one, plus audio bandwidth - which is why it is metered harder than text. Fantasy GF charges 8 tokens per minute for voice calls (4 on Ultra), which turns the 100 monthly tokens on its entry blueprint into about 12 minutes of call time. SpicyChat, for its part, only adds text-to-speech at its top tier. Latency engineering and unit economics are the same problem here: faster pipelines cost less per call, and cheaper calls are what make voice viable below the top plan.

Tier details below come from each app's own pricing or documentation pages, checked November 16, 2026, and cross-checked against il.ly's AI companion testing guide, which hands-tests 15 companion apps across memory, media, and voice.

Recent findings suggest that two takeaways from the table. First, nobody sells a bigger base model - they sell a bigger window into the same one. Second, the free tiers are deliberately memory-poor: limited context and short retention are the upgrade prompt.

Even if you never build a companion, these apps are a useful reference architecture for any stateful LLM product:.

It has been revealed that consumer AI companions have turned three hard infrastructure problems - bounded context, durable memory, and real-time voice - into their pricing pages. Context size, memory depth, and voice access are the tiers. If you are building anything stateful on an LLM, this category is worth watching closely: it is solving continuity and latency problems at consumer scale, in public, one subscription tier at a time.

Sources indicate that it is the total amount of text, measured in tokens, that the model can consider when writing its next reply. The character definition, stored memories, recent chat, and the newly introduced message all share that budget. When the conversation exceeds it, the oldest content drops out and the companion appears to forget.

Industry observers note that yes, through a memory system separate from the context window. Apps summarize older chats, extract stable facts about you into a profile, and retrieve relevant past moments into the prompt. Retention varies: some free tiers delete chat history after as little as 7 days of inactivity, while paid aims typically keep memory for the membership period.

According to recent reports, A voice turn runs three models - speech-to-text, the LLM, and text-to-speech - instead of one, plus audio transfer. Providers pass that cost on through per-minute token charges or by locking voice behind higher tiers.

For casual chat, 4K to 9K tokens works. For long-running roleplay or a companion expected to hold plot threads for weeks, 32K and up, or a well-built memory layer on top of a smaller window, makes the visible difference.

Ettin Suite: SoTA Paired Encoders and Decoders

💡 Key Takeaways
  • What would happen if you took the ModernBERT recipe and applied it to a decoder-only model?
  • Sources indicate that we introduce a upcoming open-data training recipe to reproduce the encoder-only ModernBERT model (and actually beat it!).
  • Industry observers note that this blog post introduces Ettin, the first suite of SoTA paired encoder-only and decoder-only models (17M-1B params) trained with identical data (2T tokens), architecture, and training recipes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What would happen if you took the ModernBERT recipe and applied it to a decoder-only model? Turns out, a state-of-the-art decoder language model that beats Llama 3.2 1B and SmolLM2!

Sources indicate that we introduce a upcoming open-data training recipe to reproduce the encoder-only ModernBERT model (and actually beat it!). We then apply the exact same recipe to decoder-only models. For the first time, we have two state-of-the-art models trained in the same setup but with two different training objectives: masked language modeling (MLM), and causal language modeling (CLM).

Industry observers note that this blog post introduces Ettin, the first suite of SoTA paired encoder-only and decoder-only models (17M-1B params) trained with identical data (2T tokens), architecture, and training recipes. Ettin enables true apples-to-apples comparisons between architectures and delivers state-of-the-art performance for open-data models in both categories. We then further explore whether it is possible to get a competitive encoder starting from the decoder and vice-versa.

If you are interested in trying out the models, some boilerplates are available at the end of this blogpost!

The LLM community has largely converged on decoder-only models like GPT, Llama, and Qwen. Their generative capabilities are impressive, but this focus is detracting attention from other categories, such as encoder-only models like BERT.

Industry observers note that however, encoder BERT-like models remain the workhorses of production systems for classification, retrieval, and embedding tasks. They're faster, more memory-efficient, and often more accurate for discriminative tasks. The key difference lies in their attention patterns:.

While decoder models have seen rapid innovation, encoder model development had stagnated – until recently, with efforts like ModernBERT modernizing them. But which architecture is better? Previous comparisons between encoders and decoders used different datasets, architectures, and training recipes, so it was hard to tell.

In a recent development, named after the two-headed Norse giant, Ettin provides a controlled comparison by training with both architectures on identical data, identical model shapes, and identical training recipes. They only differ in attention patterns and training objectives!

We build on the ModernBERT recipe, which borrowed modern techniques from decoder-only models and brought them to encoder training. This provides a strong base for training both architectures.

Recent findings suggest that we train six different sizes, ranging from 17M to 1B parameters. This allows us to test the effects of scale, and provides a wide variety of models for you to use! No matter if you need a blazing fast on-device model or a powerful but slower model, we got you covered!

We use a comprehensive three-phase training approach to maximize performance:.

Phase 1 - Pre-training (1.7T tokens): We start with a diverse mixture of high-quality data sources, training on shorter contexts (1024 tokens) to establish strong foundational knowledge.

Phase 2 - Context Extension (250B tokens): We increase context length to 8K tokens using higher-quality filtered data, allowing models to understand longer documents and more complex relationships.

Phase 3 - Decay (100B tokens): We finish with premium data sources including scientific papers, textbooks, and curated content while gradually reducing the learning rate.

Our encoder models gain all the benefits of ModernBERT's speed, allowing them to be significantly faster than the previous generations of encoders.

Unlike ModernBERT, all our training data is public and reproducible:.

You can continue to train these models on new data or propose a new recipe to further improve results!

Recent findings suggest that our encoder models outperform ModernBERT across all tasks and model sizes, while using completely open training data. Since we provide a large range of sizes, you can now use ModernBERT-style models in smaller sizes (great for on-device or for fast-inference), or power up with a 1B-sized encoder that crushes the competition.

Applying the same recipe to decoder models yields equally impressive results, with our models outperforming or matching established baselines such as Llama 3.2 and SmolLM2:.

The gains are particularly strong on knowledge-intensive tasks like SciQ, reflecting the benefits of our high-quality training data mixture. These results demonstrate that our training recipe creates genuinely strong models in both architectural paradigms.

Sources indicate that for the first time, we can fairly compare encoder and decoder architectures trained with identical data and recipes. The results reveal fundamental architectural advantages that persist even when all other factors are controlled:.

The results show clear patterns:.

Sources indicate that encoders dominate classification and retrieval: On MNLI classification, even a 150M encoder (89.2) outperforms a 400M decoder (88.2). For retrieval tasks, the gap is smaller but still noticeable - especially when decoders are not trained with MNTP.

Decoders excel at generation: On generative tasks, decoders maintain consistent advantages, with the performance gap actually widening at larger model sizes.

Size doesn't always matter: A 400M encoder beats a 1B decoder on classification tasks, while a 400M decoder beats a 1B encoder on generation tasks.

In a recent development, due to the lack of new encoder models, works like LLM2Vec have proposed to continue pre-training decoders with MLM. We can now test the effectiveness of this strategy!

We switched the objective and continued to train our models with the opposite objective for 50B additional tokens. This is what we found:.

This suggests the architecture choice matters fundamentally, not just the training objective.

It has been revealed that with identical training data, we can study how different objectives affect learning. For example, analyzing gender bias using the WinoGender benchmark reveals:.

This opens doors for systematic studies of how training objectives influence model behavior beyond just accuracy metrics.

For text generation tasks, use decoder models:.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Online casinos supplied most of the growth in Pennsylvania's October 2026 gaming revenue, while sports betting handle slipped. The results land as a stalled bill to ban sweepstakes casinos and raise sports betting taxes runs out of time.

Pennsylvania’s gaming revenue reached $634.4 million in October 2026, up 6.3% from a year earlier and the highest monthly total on record. Online casinos contributed a record $278.8 million, up 11.1%. The total cleared the previous single-month mark of $625.5 million, which was set in May 2026.

Sources indicate that iGaming accounted for about $27.7 million of the $37.4 million year-over-year increase. A year earlier, online casino revenue was $251,097,586, itself a record at the time. Total gaming tax revenue in October 2025 was $252,287,937, against a record $274 million this October.

It has been revealed that two licensees led the iGaming field. Hollywood Casino at Penn National generated $114.4 million, up 16%. Valley Forge Casino Resort followed with $75.2 million, up 5.3%.

Recent findings suggest that october was a stronger month than September. In September, total gaming revenue was $555,036,870, a 4.07% year-over-year increase. iGaming table revenue slipped 0.63% that month.

It has been revealed that the October pattern mirrors the last fiscal year. iGaming revenue in fiscal 2025/26 was $2,933,453,989, an 18.42% gain over the prior year. It generated $1,337,414,660 in tax. Combined gaming revenue reached $7,005,987,435, an all-time fiscal-year high. Taxes and fees returned to the state totaled $3,098,193,583.

Pennsylvania’s online casino growth is in line with a slowing iGaming trend nationally. US iGaming revenue rose 12.3% year over year to $1.03 billion in August 2026. For the state budget, the vertical is now a central source of gaming tax.

Industry observers note that sports betting moved the other way on volume. Handle fell to $903 million from $968.5 million in October 2025. Revenue still rose, to $65.1 million from $60.7 million. The same split indicated up across fiscal 2025/26. Handle dropped from $8,721,795,533 to $8,448,101,928. Sports wagering revenue rose 35.95% to $662,947,631.

According to recent reports, the record arrives as Harrisburg weighs a gaming modernization package. Rep. Russ Diamond introduced House Bill 2801 with four co-sponsors. On September 24, 2026, it was referred to the House Gaming Oversight Committee. Titled ‘Skill Games & Gaming Modernization,’ the bill would rewrite large parts of the state’s gaming code.

In a recent development, house Bill 2801 would make operating or promoting online sweepstakes games illegal in Pennsylvania. Fines would range from $50,000 to $500,000 per violation.

According to recent reports, the bill would also raise the sports wagering tax from 34% to 36%. The state right now taxes online slots at 54%. A higher sports rate would apply to a product whose handle is shrinking even as its revenue climbs.

Recent findings suggest that the bill has not moved. HB 2801 had no recorded committee hearing or vote as of mid-November, according to Legal Sports Report. The legislative session ends November 30. Bills that do not pass by then do not carry into 2027.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that gradio is an open-source Python package for creating AI-powered web applications.
  • To that end, here are some of the big improvements we've added to Gradio MCP servers as of version 5.38.0.
  • If you've tried to use a remote Gradio MCP server that takes a file as input (image, video, audio), you've probably encountered this error:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that gradio is an open-source Python package for creating AI-powered web applications. Gradio is compliant with the MCP server protocol and powers thousands of MCP servers hosted on Hugging Face Spaces. The Gradio team is betting big on Gradio and Spaces being the best way to build and host AI-powered MCP servers.

To that end, here are some of the big improvements we've added to Gradio MCP servers as of version 5.38.0.

If you've tried to use a remote Gradio MCP server that takes a file as input (image, video, audio), you've probably encountered this error:.

This happens because the Gradio server is hosted on a different machine, meaning any input files must be accessible via a public URL so they can be downloaded remotely.

According to recent reports, while many ways exist to host files online, they all add a manual step to your workflow. In the age of LLM agents, shouldn't we expect them to handle this for you?

Industry observers note that gradio now includes a "File Upload" MCP server that agents can use to upload files directly to your Gradio application. If any tools in your Gradio MCP server require file inputs, the connection documentation will now show you how to start the "File Upload" MCP server:.

Learn more about using this server (and crucial security considerations) in the Gradio Guides.

Depending on the AI task, getting results can take some time. Now, Gradio streams progress notifications to your MCP client, allowing you to monitor the status in real-time!

According to recent reports, as an MCP developer, it's highly recommended to implement your MCP tools to emit these progress statuses. Our guide shows you how.

Industry observers note that if you want to integrate an existing backend API into an LLM, you have to manually map API endpoints to MCP tools. This can be a time-consuming and error prone chore. With this release, Gradio can automate the entire process for you! With a single line of code, you can integrate your business backend into any MCP-compatible LLM.

OpenAPI is a widely adopted standard for describing RESTful APIs in a machine-readable format, typically as a JSON file. Gradio now features the gr.load_openapi function, which creates a Gradio application directly from an OpenAPI schema. You can then launch the app with mcp_server=True to automatically create an MCP server for your API!

Find more details in the Gradio Guides.

A common pattern in MCP server development is to use authentication headers to call services on behalf of your users. As an MCP server developer, you want to clearly communicate to your users which credentials they need to provide for proper server usage.

To make this possible, you can now type your MCP server arguments as gr.Header. Gradio will automatically extract that header from the incoming request (if it exists) and pass it to your function. The benefit of using gr.Header is that the MCP connection docs will automatically display the headers you need to supply when connecting to the server!

In the example below, the X-API-Token header is extracted from the incoming request and passed in as the x_api_token argument to make_api_request_on_behalf_of_user.

You can read more about this in the Gradio Guides.

According to recent reports, gradio automatically generates tool descriptions from your function names and docstrings. Now you can customize the tool description even further with the api_description parameter. In this example, the tool description will read "Apply a sepia filter to any image.".

Industry observers note that want us to add a upcoming MCP-related feature to Gradio? Let us know in the comments of the blog or on GitHub. Also if you've built a cool MCP server or Gradio app let us know in the comments and we'll amplify it!
